articles.title: Hanwha Highlights M38/M48 MUSV and Containerized Munitions at AUSA 2026
articles.text:
At AUSA 2026, Hanwha Defense USA featured a model of the M38 MUSV made in partnership with Magnet Defense, with the parent design vessel recently arriving at National Harbor just outside of Washington D.C. following previous rounds of testing at sea.

Hanwha’s Kevin Schoonover provided insight into the ongoing program, including several of Hanwha’s munitions offering destined to outfit the vessel and other platforms, alongside greater detail pertaining to the partnership with Magnet Defense. Schoonover also highlighted how the M38 is the primary testing vehicle for the class standing at 38 meters long, with future production upgrading to the larger 48 meter standard found on the M48. To this end steel has been cut for the first M48, with production coinciding with continued testing of the original M38.

Naval News previously reported on the partnership between Hanwha and Magnet Defense, primarily geared towards breaching the emerging U.S. USV market. Schoonover also detailed how Hanwha handles most of the construction on the vessel along with work regarding autonomous weapons integration, whilst Magnet Defense handles most of the autonomy in regards to navigation and the vessel’s actual operation.

Like similar sized USVs, the M38 also features the capability to carry containerized payloads related to multiple missions, including strike, reconnaissance, and electronic warfare. M38 has already demonstrated its range of 17,000 nautical miles on multiple tests, including a trip across the Pacific to American Samoa in up to conditions of Sea State 9 . This has been part of a bid to introduce the M38 to overseas markets, including those beyond the U.S.’s MUSV program and Korean operation.

M38’s Weapons

Joining the M38 at Hanwha’s booth, the company showcased offerings for both containerized Multiple Launch Rocket Systems (MLRS) and containerized Vertical Launch Systems (VLS). There are a total of 4 different containerized systems on display, with two systems fitting inside of a 20 foot long shipping containers and the others using 40 foot standard shipping containers. When paired with M38, the vessel can carry up to 4 of the 20 foot long containerized munition packages, 2 of the 40 foot long options, or a combination of a pair of 20 foot containers and a singular 40 foot container

A containerized version of the Chunmoo family of MLRS systems constitutes one of the 20 foot options, utilizing the same munitions and launch mechanisms found on the truck based version. This enables carriage of 2 MLRS pods, with each pod containing up to 6 CGR-080 guided rockets, 4 CTM-MR ballistic missiles (with a range of 160km), 4 CTM-160 Anti-Ship Ballistic Missiles, 1 CTM-290 Ballistic Missile (with a range of 290km), or 1 CTM-X Ballistic Missile featuring a range of 500 kilometers.

The other containers represent Hanwha’s iterations on containerized VLS systems, with the other 20 foot container featuring a shortened K-VLS compact system, with 4 cells primarily meant for smaller surface to air missile systems such as K-SAAM. The two 40 foot options carry 4 cells of K-VLS I or 2 cells of K-VLS II respectively. The container with K-VLS I can employ Red Shark rocket launched torpedoes (K-ASROC), SSM-700K type surface to surface cruise missiles, and K-SAAM. The container with K-VLS II can utilize the larger L-SAM (intended to replace the SM-2 in Korean service), and other larger ballistic and cruise missiles.

articles.title: European U740 Variant Of The XQ-58A Valkyrie Has Flown
articles.text:
Airbus and Kratos Defense & Security Solutions have completed the first flight of the U740 Valkyrie uncrewed combat aircraft, a Europeanized version of the XQ-58A Valkyrie, advancing their bid to deliver a combat-ready system to Germany by 2029. The flight comes as the German Air Force, or Luftwaffe, moves toward acquiring a new class of jet-powered combat drones, in what could become a major shift in the country’s traditionally limited armed-uncrewed-aircraft capabilities.

The flight took place at an unnamed test facility in northern Europe, Airbus announced on October 12. The aircraft conducted a rocket-assisted takeoff, maneuvers at different altitudes, and flight at speeds of up to Mach 0.8. The test also included in-flight mission adjustments, with Airbus reporting that all objectives were met.

The next phase will introduce Airbus’ Multi-platform Autonomous Reconfigurable and Secure (MARS) mission system, which is intended to provide the aircraft’s European-controlled software and mission-management architecture. Airbus says MARS will support autonomous operations and coordination between multiple uncrewed aircraft while retaining human oversight of critical decisions.

The U740 is based on Kratos’ American-developed XQ-58A, an uncrewed aircraft designed as a relatively affordable combat platform. Airbus is adapting the aircraft with its MARS mission system and presenting the combination as a way to provide Germany with a sovereign European capability without waiting for an entirely new airframe to mature.

Published performance figures for the U740 include a maximum takeoff weight of around 3,000 kilograms (6,600 pounds). Airbus lists a range exceeding 5,000 kilometers (3,100 miles) and a service ceiling of 45,000 feet. It has an internal weapons bay and external payload stations beneath its wings.

One distinctive feature is the U740’s rocket-assisted launch capability, which reduces its dependence on conventional runways. The original Valkyrie design is primarily recovered by parachute, but newer versions can take off with rocket assistance and land on a runway, offering greater flexibility in how and where they operate. That could help the Luftwaffe disperse operations or launch aircraft from locations where established airfields are unavailable or under threat. The XQ-58 family has also shown some potential for scaling to different requirements, as detailed in these earlier reports on runway launch and recovery and further platform development. In particular, the U.S. Marine Corps has been exploring ways to expand the XQ-58’s flexibility, including further development of the Valkyrie to meet its own mission requirements.

If adopted, the rocket-assisted launch capability would provide an intriguing throwback to practical German studies during the Cold War, in which F-104G Starfighter fighter-bombers used the Zero-Length Launch (ZELL) system to take off from dispersed locations.

Airbus says the U740 will be able to operate autonomously or under the direction of crewed fighters such as the Eurofighter. The company sees it as a means of increasing the reach, firepower, and survivability of existing combat aircraft, with uncrewed platforms undertaking higher-risk missions.

With the MARS system, Airbus intends to give European customers control over mission applications, data, and key software functions, while enabling autonomous mission execution and coordination between aircraft. This is particularly relevant for Germany, which will likely want to integrate national weapons, sensors, and operational requirements without becoming dependent on a foreign-controlled mission architecture.

Since the underlying airframe is American, the degree of sovereignty Germany ultimately obtains will depend on the practical ability to control and modify software, integrate national systems, and support the aircraft throughout its service life.

The European flight is an important step for the Valkyrie program, but substantial work remains before it can be considered combat-ready. Mission-system integration, further testing, and the demonstration of effective cooperation with crewed aircraft will be central to meeting the companies’ 2029 target.

The effort is also unfolding as Germany develops its requirements for what has been described in press reports as a Jagdbomberdrohne, or fighter-bomber drone. The precise operational concept has yet to emerge publicly, including whether the Luftwaffe primarily wants an uncrewed aircraft to accompany crewed fighters or a platform capable of conducting independent long-range strike missions.

Germany has historically lagged behind several other major military powers in fielding armed uncrewed aircraft. Previous attempts to acquire larger reconnaissance drones encountered major technical and procurement difficulties, while political resistance to armed drones delayed the development of a strike capability for years.

The Luftwaffe’s current larger uncrewed aircraft fleet remains limited to five leased Israeli-made Heron TP medium-altitude, long-endurance drones. Germany is also participating in the Eurodrone program, while uncrewed systems were expected to form part of the wider Future Combat Air System (FCAS), before that Franco-German-led effort hit the buffers earlier this year.

Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and Germany’s subsequent military buildup have intensified pressure to address these gaps. Berlin has set a goal of being ready for war by 2029, and reports indicate that the Luftwaffe wants a new combat-drone capability on a similarly ambitious timeline.

As well as Airbus and Kratos, the emerging competition reportedly includes Anduril, General Atomics partnered with Germany’s INTEC, as well as Lockheed Martin. Boeing and Rheinmetall are meanwhile pitching the larger, Block 3 version of the Australian-developed MQ-28 Ghost Bat, while Helsing and Hensoldt are pursuing the homegrown CA-1 Europa.

The various proposals reflect a broader shift toward uncrewed aircraft that can deliver additional weapons, sensors, and electronic warfare capabilities without putting a pilot at risk. But Germany’s terminology raises an important question about the intended role.

A conventional collaborative combat aircraft, or CCA, would be designed to work alongside crewed fighters, extending their reach and providing additional combat mass. A platform intended to operate independently against targets deep inside enemy territory would place greater emphasis on range and survivability. These roles are not mutually exclusive, but the Luftwaffe’s final requirements will shape the aircraft it chooses.

Germany may not be looking for a single drone to do everything. One option might be a split high-low approach that could pair more capable, longer-range systems for deep-strike missions with cheaper, attritable collaborative combat aircraft that can fly alongside crewed fighters. At this point, it should also be noted that CCAs could also give older fourth-generation fighters a new lease on life, boosting their lethality and survivability by extending their sensor reach, adding weapons capacity, and allowing uncrewed aircraft to take on more dangerous tasks.

Meanwhile, Airbus is also working on its larger U760 Ravenstorm, intended for service in the early 2030s. The Ravenstorm gives Airbus a longer-term path toward a more advanced European-designed uncrewed combat aircraft as it pursues the nearer-term Valkyrie effort.

In the short term, the Luftwaffe will need to determine which capabilities must be available in an initial operational fleet and which can be introduced later. Even an aircraft based on an established design requires substantial integration, testing, training, and infrastructure before it can be employed effectively in combat.

Germany’s 2029 target leaves little time for a program that still has to integrate its mission system and demonstrate how the aircraft will be used operationally. That is a particular challenge for the Luftwaffe, which has little experience operating large uncrewed aircraft, let alone jet-powered systems intended for combat.

The European flight gives Airbus and Kratos a head start in testing the U740 for German requirements, but the next major milestone will be flying it with the MARS mission system. How quickly that work progresses will help determine whether the Valkyrie can meet the Luftwaffe’s timetable.

articles.title: Russia was not ready for the data center war it started with Ukraine
articles.text:
When Russia began attacking Ukrainian data centers and telecommunication infrastructure, it apparently failed to prepare for possible retaliation. Now Russia’s digital services are facing widespread outages after Ukrainian drone strikes knocked out three of the largest data centers owned by Russian tech giant Yandex within several days.

Pro-Kremlin bloggers are warning that Russia’s centralized digital economy could collapse because the country is not prepared for the “data center war” it started, according to posts translated by the pseudonymous independent researcher ChrisO_wiki. The Russian commentators also suggested that Ukraine’s decentralized digital services could prove more resilient than Russia’s system if the countries continue trading such blows.

Russia initially launched a drone strike campaign targeting Ukrainian data centers and mobile phone networks in late September. The attacks temporarily disrupted Internet and cell phone service for up to 100,000 households in the Ukrainian capital of Kyiv and came as part of a broader long-range strike campaign that has involved Russian missiles and jet-powered drones hitting Ukraine’s power grid infrastructure, transportation hubs, and even residential apartment building blocks.

articles.title: This Is Our First Look At The Wolf Armored Fighting Vehicle That Aims To Replace The Bradley
articles.text:
General Dynamics Land Systems (GDLS) has offered the first official look at its proposal to replace the U.S. Army’s Bradley Fighting Vehicles, called the Wolf. The Wolf is one of two designs competing to become the Army’s future XM30 Mechanized Infantry Combat Vehicle (MICV). Just earlier today, we published a detailed update on the XM30 competition, including new information about both entrants and the Army’s testing plans, which you can find here.

GDLS is showing the one-eighth-scale model of Wolf, seen at the top of this story and made by a company called KiwiMill, at the Association of the U.S. Army’s (AUSA) main annual convention, at which TWZ is in attendance. Wolf is facing off head-to-head against a version of the Lynx from Germany’s Rheinmetall, supplied via the company’s U.S. subsidiary, American Rheinmetall.

It has already been established that Wolf is a further evolution of the GDLS’ Griffin III design, which was first shown publicly at AUSA back in 2018. Griffin III was derived from the ASCOD 2 infantry fighting vehicle, for which Spain was the launch customer, and which is now entering service in Latvia. The U.S. Army’s now-cancelled M10 Booker ‘light tank’ and the British Army’s much-troubled Ajax are also members of this broader family of armored vehicles.

The design of the Wolf, at least based on the model, is substantially different from the earlier Griffin III demonstrator.

Wolf’s turret has a broader, flatter, and overall more streamlined shape, which is in line with its remotely-operated design. There is just a single sensor turret on top, along with space for a forward-looking sensor suite to the left of the main 50mm cannon. What may be apertures for additional sensors or other systems are seen elsewhere along the front and sides of the turret. It also has more launchers for smoke grenades around the front edges compared to the Griffin III.

Compared to the Griffin III, the Wolf’s hull has also been much revised, including the elimination of a traditional driver’s hatch in front of the turret ring. The vehicle’s commander (who also acts as the gunner) and driver sit side-by-side deeper inside the hull. Up to six passengers can ride in a compartment further at the rear. For comparison, the Bradley has a crew of three, as well as the ability to carry six passengers.

The Wolf’s hull also features side skirts that were not found on the Griffin III demonstrator. A different style of tracks is also depicted on the model. The picture of the model that GDLS shared shows sensors facing outward from a position on the side of the hull toward the front, as well. This makes sense, as the design features a distributed camera system to offer a full 360-degree view of the outside to personnel riding within, the broad benefits of which you can read more about here.

“Because we have a reduced crew from the Bradley [which has a commander and gunner in turret] there has to be greater efficiency in how those soldiers execute their tasks,” Geoffrey Norman, GDLS’ director for U.S. Strategy & Growth, previously noted to TWZ. “The software and menu logic are very intuitive.”

Next-generation fire control, sensor, and networking/communications capabilities, as well as improved active and passive defenses, are key requirements for the XM30 program. Both Wolf and American Rheinmetall Lynx-based designs have built-in launchers for loitering munitions, with GDLS having chosen to integrate AeroVironment’s Switchblade 300 more specifically. What we have seen on the Wolf model so far does not appear to explicitly show this particular feature.

Wolf and Lynx both also feature hybrid-electric propulsion, which will bring various benefits, especially in terms of fuel economy and electrical power generation, compared to the diesel-engined Bradley. When it comes to the boost in on-board electrical power, “the emphasis from the Army has really been about having margin on the vehicle for future [system] requirements – directed energy, counter-UAS systems, or fill-in-the-blank,” GDLS’ Norman has also told us in the past.

As it stands now, both GDLS and American Rheinmetall have delivered prototypes of their respective designs to the Army, with initial testing having been conducted at Aberdeen Proving Ground in Maryland. Soldier touchpoints and field evaluations are now set to occur at Fort Hood in Texas between February and March of next year. You can read in more detail about both entrants in the XM30 competition and what is known about their features in our past reporting here.

In the meantime, we have now gotten clear views of both designs vying to become the Army’s XM30 replacement for the venerable Bradley.

Contact the author: joe@twz.com

articles.text:
For over a decade now, the only "official" way to play Hideo Kojima's cult classic, P.T.—the long-discontinued "playable trailer" for Kojima's canceled "Silent Hills" project—has been via one of the increasingly rare PlayStation 4s that previously downloaded a copy during its monthslong availability window. Now, though, one coder is helping to preserve the game with a porting tool that builds a playable x86 PC executable from the original PS4 files.

Coder Lorean Xavier said he was inspired to work on the "P.T. for PC" project "because P.T. deserved to keep existing somewhere other than on consoles that still have it installed." The open source porting effort rebuilds the P.T. engine in C++ and Vulkan, using the original files from the PS4 game to re-create "every level, model, texture, sound, script and cutscene," according to its GitHub listing. That means players without their own legitimate decrypted copy of the original P.T. will have to track one down in order to generate a playable PC version.

The reliance on real P.T. files makes this port more authentic than previous hobbyist efforts to re-create the look and feel of P.T. for a PC audience. And while PS4 emulators recently reached a point where they could run P.T. completely, this native port also sports extra features, like upscaling and frame-generation, a camera mode, experimental third-person and VR support, and a "museum" section where you can look at and listen to in-game assets (including "unused content").

articles.title: AMD unveils Helion racks for AI agents at OCP summit
articles.text: AMD is expanding its rack-scale AI lineup with a design to run AI agents, offering CPU-only configurations or integrated CPU/GPU deployments, and liquid-cooled or air-cooled versions. Revealed at the Open Compute Project (OCP) Summit 2026 in San Jose, California, the chipmaker's new rack reference design is named Helion, while its existing system carries the moniker Helios, which we can't help feeling is inviting confusion a little. Helion offers an OCP-compliant blueprint for agentic AI infrastructure built around AMD's CPUs and accelerators. AMD launched Helios earlier this year for frontier-scale AI training and large-scale inference. Helion's enterprise configuration instead combines agent execution and inference within a single rack. Customers can opt for a CPU-only hyperscale configuration or an enterprise configuration with a mix of CPU and GPU blades. Depending on configuration, AMD advertises up to 32,768 of AMD's "Zen 6" CPU cores, delivered via compute nodes fitted with 256-core versions of its Venice Epyc processor, up to 16 of its Instinct MI350P GPU accelerators, and up to 102 Tbps of networking bandwidth. The CPU-only hyperscale version offers dedicated capacity for agent execution and connections to separate model inference infrastructure, while the enterprise configuration combines agent execution, GPU inference, and supporting workloads in one rack. Both configurations offer dense, balanced, or high-performance CPU blades. For dense deployments, EPYC 9006 chips rated at 400 W are used, while performance blades sport a version of the chip with just 96 cores but clocked at 5 GHz. Balanced blades use 256-core processors rated at 600 W. There are also GPU inference blades, with eight Instinct MI350P GPUs in a 5U server, plus general-purpose blades, intended for database and storage servers or technical compute workloads. AMD SVP for Compute and Enterprise AI Dan McNamara said agentic AI is not a single workload, spanning enterprise applications and complex workflows, each with different compute requirements. "To do that takes optimized compute and infrastructure that can adapt to different workloads. With AMD Helion, we are bringing Epyc performance, open software and flexible rack designs together so our partners can build systems around customer needs and make efficient use of available power," he added. AMD says it plans to contribute the Helion specifications to OCP, making them available to the community for further development and adoption. Partner-built Helion configurations are scheduled for November 2026. In its announcement, AMD cites Cisco, Dell, HPE, Foxconn, Lenovo, Supermicro, and others as on board with the new kit. ®

articles.text:
Mohammed Yousuf Ali, an Indian techie who died in the attack on Riyadh airport, had called his family to Saudi Arabia for ‘Umrah’ and they were about to leave for the holy city of Madina when the airport came under attack.
Yousuf Ali (46), an IT engineer from Hyderabad employed in Riyadh for the last 10 years, had called his wife and three children to Saudi Arabia about 10 days ago to perform ‘Umrah’ (mini pilgrimage).
According to information received by his relatives here, Yusuf Ali, his wife, two sons, a daughter and his aunt were at King Khalid International Airport on Sunday. As they were waiting in the lounge to board a flight to Madina, the airport was hit by a missile fired by Houthis.
The debris fell on Yousuf, his family members and other ‘Umrah’ pilgrims. The techie was critically injured and was admitted to a hospital, where he later succumbed.
The Indian embassy in Riyadh on Sunday night confirmed that an Indian died in the attack.
Yousuf’s sons — 18-year-old Aman Ali and 16-year-old Wasi Ali — were injured. Aman underwent knee surgery while his brother lost three of his toes. Both are students in Hyderabad.
The techie’s wife, Sameera, and their 11-year-old daughter, Maryam, a student of Class 6 in a school in Hyderabad, escaped with minor injuries.
On receipt of the information about Yousuf’s death, his relatives and friends reached his residence at Mehdipatnam.
One of the relatives said the last rites of Yousuf are likely to be performed in Riyadh.
Hyderabad MP Asaduddin Owaisi urged Minister for External Affairs S. Jaishankar to provide every possible assistance to the family.
The MP said he was in touch with Yousuf’s brother-in-law in Riyadh.
Another man from Telangana was also injured in the attack, which claimed 13 lives and left 300 injured.
Shaik Saeed (42) from Kamareddy district, who was employed at a café at the airport, was injured when the debris fell on him. He was reportedly admitted to King Fahad Military Hospital and was undergoing treatment in the intensive care unit.
Saeed’s two brothers are also employed in Saudi Arabia.
Eleven Indians were among those injured in the attack.

“Our Embassy officials have visited all hospitals where Indian nationals injured in the attack have been admitted. As mentioned earlier, 1 Indian national unfortunately passed away today, 3 are in ICU but stable, 2 more are admitted in normal wards while others have been discharged,” the Embassy said.
“We thank the Saudi authorities for the medical care provided to the injured Indian nationals and assure the families that the Embassy will provide all possible support,” it added.

articles.title: Chinese Seller Offers Retired MiG-29 Engines as Scrap
articles.text:
A Chinese online seller has advertised 9 retired Klimov RD-33 jet engines previously used on MiG-29 fighter aircraft for a combined asking price of ¥550,000 with shipping included. The listing described the engines as being in good condition for aviation training and modification, but provided no evidence to confirm their airworthiness.
The advertisement placed by the account, identified as VH Aviation (VH), contained images of multiple engines stored in the open yard. Their condition and presentation suggest that they are more likely to be offered for disposal as retired equipment rather than a source of power.
Whether the engines are being advertised for sale as scrap was not established by the advertisement. The Chinese-language listing identified the equipment as Klimov RD-33 aircraft engines and stated that the units had been retired from service. The asking price of ¥550,000 was not independently established by the listing to cover the sale all 9 engines, or to indicate other conditions of sale.
The photographs depicted used turbofan engines with signs of weathering and exposed external condition. They do not establish the engines’ internal condition, completeness or remaining service life.
No engine serial numbers, operating-hour records, overhaul documentation or inspection certificates were visible in the supplied material.
The RD-33 turbofan engine was developed by the Soviet Union’s Klimov design bureau for the MiG-29 family of fighter aircraft. The engine has powered several versions of the aircraft, including variants operated by the Indian Air Force.
An engine’s retirement from military service does not imply that it has reached the technical end of its life. Depending on its condition, a retired engine might continue to be used for training, be dismantled for parts, or be sold for material recovery.
However, the Chinese listing does not provide sufficient information to confirm any of these uses for each engine. Its reference to training and modification does not constitute verification of serviceability.
If the engines are incomplete, beyond economical repair or lacking documentation for restoration, this might make them valuable as training equipment, spare parts or scrap material. This assertion by the seller would need to be backed by a physical inspection and verification of claims by the seller.

articles.text: Microsoft has closed a loophole that let users sidestep the need for an account during setup for consumer versions of Windows 11. Microsoft requires an account during initial setup of Windows 11 Home and Pro for personal use. Defence technology companies can participate in two near-term government-led initiatives in India and the United States, one of which is a US-sponsored challenge seeking proposals for low-cost intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance (ISR) and another is an Indian invitation to technology partners for defence projects.
The US Defense Innovation Unit (DIU) has scheduled 14 October 2026 as the deadline for the submissions to its Low-Cost ISR Challenge. articles.text:
Formula 1’s lengthy 2026 season is entering its final stretch. The sport took to the floodlit streets of Singapore on Sunday night, but Saturday saw action, too; this Grand Prix weekend was also the final of six sprints this year. The night race might be one of modern F1’s greatest spectacles. From overhead shots, the track becomes a bright, illuminated ribbon among the looming darkness of the city-state’s overpasses and skyscrapers. At ground level, the cars shower glittering sparks from their titanium skid blocks as the drivers flirt with how close they can get to the walls. As tracks go, the 90-degree turns and concrete barrier-lined streets were a world away from the abrasive tarmac and ample runoff of Malaysia last time out. But the tropical heat and humidity were a constant given both locations’ proximity to the equator.

Showers for the sprint

In Malaysia (which was still technically the Bahrain GP), a pre-race downpour disrupted things mightily. On Saturday morning in Singapore, shortly before the start of the sprint, it seemed history was about to rhyme when the skies opened. With standing water in places on the track, the sprint was delayed by 30 minutes. The sprint format, where a short extra race replaces a practice session a day before the main event, is unloved by the drivers and teams. For one thing, there’s little prestige in winning Saturday’s sprint. And with qualifying just a few hours later, risk-taking is discouraged lest one wreck the car and ruin Sunday’s race a day early.

Oh no, not again! Credit: Mark Thompson/Getty Images

And in Singapore, like most street circuits, the proximity of the unyielding barriers that line the track means there are real, punishing consequences for getting it even a little wrong.

articles.title: Astrome Wins Indian Army’s iDEX Challenge for Man-Portable ELINT System
articles.text:
Bengaluru-based defence technology company Astrome has won the Indian Army and Defence Innovation Organisation’s (DIO) iDEX DISC 14 challenge to develop a next generation, man-portable Electronic Intelligence (ELINT) system with Electronic Support Measures (ESM) capabilities.
The system is for tactical electronic warfare and wideband threat detection including high-altitude and forward-border areas. Astrome announced the win in a company graphic, calling it another iDEX challenge milestone. The problem statement for this particular call has been uploaded on the official iDEX portal of DISC 14.
The proposed system is intended to overcome the shortcomings of traditional ELINT equipment, which include limited frequency coverage, bulkier design, and insufficient direction-finding accuracy.
A man-portable system would allow Army personnel to carry the equipment to locations where larger, vehicle-mounted systems may not be feasible. Especially in high-altitude and forward-border areas, mobility often plays a key role in military operations.
The iDEX challenge calls for improved direction-finding performance, expanded signal coverage, and increased modularity to meet the evolving demands of electronic-warfare operations.
ELINT systems are used to gather and analyse electronic emissions; ESM capabilities, meanwhile, assist in detecting, identifying, and analysing signals that may reveal the presence of hostile radars or other emitters.
The proposed platform is expected to integrate precision direction-finding and real-time signal processing capabilities; these would help identify and locate emitters and provide valuable information to help make tactical decisions. Especially in the age of modern electronic warfare, where radar technology, communication links, and other electronic systems are becoming increasingly important, such equipment is crucial to detect, identify, and locate such emissions.
The award falls under the Defence India Startup Challenge (DISC) — part of the Ministry of Defence’s iDEX initiative — which promotes start-ups, MSMEs, and innovators who could develop technologies that have potential application in India’s armed forces.

articles.title: Ukrainian drone strikes on Yandex datacenters knock cloud and payments offline
articles.text: Yandex engineers are working to restore services after Ukraine launched drone strikes on three of its five Russian datacenters. The strikes began overnight on October 7-8, "seriously damaging" Yandex's Sasovo datacenter and leading to a total shutdown. Ukrainian drones struck again on the morning of October 9, targeting the company's Kaluga datacenter, resulting in part of its infrastructure being taken offline. Dima Pirogov, head of Yandex's fintech division, confirmed via Telegram on Sunday morning that a third strike targeted the company's Vladimir site, which supports Yandex Pay. A day later, services remain offline, although Pirogov said users' money is safe. "I'm very sorry I can't tell you yet that everything is working again," the exec wrote. "The team continues to restore services and is checking every step. When it comes to your money, it's important to us not just to restore Yandex Pay as quickly as possible, but also to ensure that everything is working reliably. "I understand that you're not waiting for words, but for access to your money. And I understand how hard it is to wait when you can't use it. We can't give you a precise timeline for the restoration yet, but we promise: we won't stop until the service is back online." Yandex Pay is the company's digital payments service. Users can make online and in-store purchases, pay in installments, and split bills with friends and family. It's also integrated into online shopping experiences. It is comparable to Apple Pay or Google Pay, while Yandex more broadly offers services similar to Google's. Yandex said engineers are prioritizing the most-used services, and reported that access to the Alice AI assistant, Mail, Maps, Search, and Taxi is being restored, but other features remain offline. The company's status page lists widespread outages across Yandex Cloud, its public cloud platform, following the attacks. Updates from the maintenance team describe partial availability despite the outage indicators. They suggest that some customers may be able to access certain features, such as Yandex Cloud Console and API, but availability remains inconsistent across the platform. In its most recent update, the company said: "The Yandex Cloud platform is still operating in a limited mode. Our specialists continue restoration work around the clock. The technical support team receives an increased number of requests, so the response time can be increased. "Our recommendations continue to be relevant. We recommend using alternative sites for hosting and reserving resources." Internet monitoring organization Netblocks reported that Yandex Cloud's network connectivity was at 30 percent of normal levels on October 11. Ukraine president Volodymyr Zelensky said the drone attacks were a response to Russia's own, which had targeted datacenters in Kyiv. The BBC reported that in September, Russian drone strikes targeted a business center in the capital city, killing four people and damaging a datacenter, which in turn resulted in around 100,000 households losing internet access. The attacks led to other knock-on effects, such as public transport boards not displaying information in Lutsk. Kyiv's attack on the Vladimir site on Sunday morning came hours after controversial comments from US president Donald Trump, who accused Zelensky of wanting "to make problems for the world" by continuing to attack Russian oil refineries. Trump went on to say that it was time for Ukraine to elect a new president after Zelensky said measures should not be taken that allow Russia to generate more revenue to fund its war. Zelensky was referring to a deal between Trump and Putin to release diesel from Russia to the US and the rest of the world. Later that day, the US president claimed Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an "energy ceasefire" to halt attacks on each other's energy infrastructure. Kyiv said it was unaware of the agreement before Trump announced it on his social media platform, but was willing to halt attacks on Russian energy infrastructure if Moscow reciprocated. Russia launched a missile attack on a Ukrainian power plant hours later. ®

articles.title: Chinese Pilots Say Rafale Has Edge Over J-16, Boosting India’s Case for More Jets
articles.text:
Chinese fighter pilots reportedly acknowledged the Dassault Rafale’s superiority in the close-range manouevring against China’s Shenyang J-16 during the Eagles of Civilization 2026 air exercise in Egypt. The report appeared in the media on 11 October. If correct, the pilots’ comments provide an interesting perspective on how Chinese crews were impressed by the French jet during the rare opportunity to engage its aircraft in combat training.
The exercise, held by the Chinese and Egyptian air forces in August and September, involved the first ever training engagements of China’s J-16 against Egypt’s Rafales and MiG-29M/M2 fighters. Chinese military media reported details of medium- and close-range air-to-air combat drills, but neither Beijing nor Cairo released an official scorecard of which fighter had been victorious in the engagements.
The Rafale’s delta-canard design and digital flight-control system enable an excellent manouverability, particularly during the most challenging close-range combat. However, the ability to turn quickly does not necessarily provide victory in a dogfight: energy management, pilot training, weapons, sensors and the tactical situation all contribute to the result of a battle.
The J-16 is a big twin-engine multirole fighter based on the Flanker design. It provides great payload capacity and long-range combat abilities, combined with advanced avionics. Despite the possible edge of the Rafale in the close-range fight, this does not mean it is superior to the J-16 in all aspects and engagements.
The issue is of interest to India, which possesses its own Rafale fighters while China has the J-16 and the cutting-edge J-20 stealth fighter. The lessons learnt from the exercise will be invaluable in understanding the strengths and weaknesses of the different platforms, as well as tactics and training.
However, Egypt’s Rafale is not the same as India’s aircraft, which integrate country-specific weapons, avionics and other modifications. Moreover, the results of training engagements depend on the pilots’ skills, the mission rules of engagement, the support of airborne early warning aircraft and electronic-warfare capabilities.
While Chinese state media shared video footage of the training engagements, the public materials do not present credible evidence of a kill ratio or show that Rafale routinely beat the J-16. Earlier reports circulating online about the alleged results of the engagements were not confirmed by either of the warring sides.
The distinction is important, as training exercises provide valuable experience for the participants. However, the outcome of exercises often depends on the rules of the engagement, the initial situation setup and the weapons used, which may not reflect real combat conditions.

articles.title: UCLA settles Oracle ERP dispute with $3.1M in credits and $1.31M wiped off the bill
articles.text: UCLA and Oracle have settled a dispute over a troubled ERP project originally budgeted at $120 million, with the vendor waiving $1.31 million in outstanding fees and granting $3.1 million in credits against future charges. In May, the University of California's Compliance and Audit Committee recommended a settlement [PDF] of UCLA's pre-litigation dispute with Oracle, which the Board of Regents approved. According to documents released in response to a California Public Records Act request, UCLA stopped paying its Oracle subscription in September 2024 over what it described as shortcomings in grants management functionality. UCLA and Oracle signed their first agreement relating to the project – called Ascend – in November 2017. The project had a revised go-live date of January 2025, but was paused in mid-2024. The settlement records UCLA's allegation that "the ERP Cloud Services did not perform as warranted in the Oracle Agreement." "The ERP Cloud Services lacked sufficient functionality to meet the University's requirements and could not be used by the University as expected," said the document, which was seen by The Register. It continued that "the University incurred costs and delays due to the ERP Cloud Services inability to meet the University's requirements." It added: "As a result, Oracle breached the Oracle Agreement." Under the settlement, UCLA agreed to pay Oracle $350,000 of the $1.66 million in outstanding invoices. Oracle then waived the remaining balance – $1.31 million – and credited $3.1 million against future Oracle fees. These credits expire at the end of May 2028. The agreement says the university should not make public statements about its terms, which are to remain confidential, although both parties acknowledged that UCLA is subject to the California Public Records Act. The Register has asked Oracle to comment. The settlement was obtained by California resident Eric Guyer, founder of independent Oracle cost consultancy Advizant. In a social media post, he said that the credits suggested UCLA would continue with the project in some form, with Oracle as the main vendor. Guyer suggested Oracle most likely discounted its software to win the "coveted" UCLA logo. He estimated the total subscription value at around $12 million over ten years. He said Oracle tends to move decisively when unpaid bills on clear contractual terms back it into a corner. "This is rare despite the lore of its litigious nature. Everyone has a line. In any case, UCLA's claim probably went to Oracle because it was the easiest to point a finger at: consultants sell effort, not outcomes, and internal staff can only be fired." However, he said the average customer should not conclude that claiming a breach and stopping payment is advisable. "It can be effective, but is an exceedingly painful path," he claimed. "In this rare case, Oracle agreed to eat some shit at the end of a poorly planned implementation in exchange for UCLA's silence in the fiercely competitive higher ed market. In other public implementation fights, Oracle struck first or countersued, with press releases to match." UCLA serves around 49,000 students and manages a budget of around $11 billion. A 2025 report [PDF] presented to the University of California Board of Regents' Finance and Capital Strategies Committee said that among the "Top Issues, Risks and Challenges" the UCLA project leadership faced was "Oracle's lack of responsiveness – particularly regarding licensing costs and support." It added that the project's original $120 million budget was revised down to $98.9 million, with $13.5 million remaining as of December 31, 2024. The report, covering the period through December 2024, said the project started in April 2018 and was originally expected to end in July 2020. The document described it as a "comprehensive business transformation initiative" to modernize the university's financial, budgetary, and research administration operations by moving to Oracle Cloud SaaS. It also included retrofitting any systems that connected with the main finance system. The procurement module, BruinBuy Plus, went live in January 2024, but the main "Oracle Financials go-live has been paused since August 2 [2024] and is undergoing program assessment," the document said. Among the mitigation plans in the review was to "finalize the decision on whether to continue with the current vendor or explore alternatives" based on a reassessment of the tool and provider. According to the settlement document, the University told Oracle via email on June 20, 2025 that the "University wanted to terminate the Ascend project and the ERP Cloud Services." In May, a spokesperson for UCLA said in a statement to The Register: "The University continues to evaluate the most effective path forward for financial systems modernization." Under the terms of the settlement agreement, the University and Oracle have agreed to make no further claims for damages related to the contract dispute, and neither has admitted liability. According to a report from campus newspaper Daily Bruin, UCLA was still using legacy financial systems software designed in the 1980s when the budget was just seven percent of its current size. It was a mainframe-based "ancient relic of a system," former project steering committee member Reem Hanna-Harwell told the newspaper. The Daily Bruin reported that at least $213 million had been spent and cited a May 2024 town hall presentation projecting total costs of roughly $286 million. ®

articles.title: Amazon has over 1 million robot workers. What’s next for human employees?
articles.text:
No organization in the world operates more robots than Amazon. The company already has more than 1 million robots working in warehouses around the clock to make tens of millions of same-day and one-day package deliveries happen on a daily basis—and Amazon is poised to significantly grow that robotic fleet in the coming years as it establishes new factories to churn out increasingly more capable robot workers.

Despite deploying so many robots, Amazon is also the second-largest corporate employer in the world, with more than 1.5 million full-time and part-time human workers, according to its 2025 annual report. Amazon executives say that the growing robot fleet has eased the burden on its human workforce by taking on the toughest fulfillment center tasks that carry the greatest risks of physical fatigue and injury. But labor advocacy groups and independent researchers point to evidence suggesting that warehouse automation driven by AI is not all upside for the humans who work alongside robots.

“For the last 100 years, most of the automation that we've seen usually happens away from workers—you're taking that high-risk task away from the worker, and you're doing so in a way that is not physically proximate,” Brian Greenwood, professor of business at George Mason University, told Ars. “The rise of collaborative robots really changes that dynamic for two reasons: one is that it is physically proximate, and two, the robot has the ability to dictate the pace of work.”

articles.title: Microsoft giveth and Microsoft taketh away: Copilot edition
articles.text: Not satisfied with shoehorning Copilot into every crevice of Office, Microsoft is adding Office to the Copilot app, while also evicting the AI assistant from certain parts of Outlook. The plan is simple: give the Copilot app a prompt, and it will create an Office document (for example, Word) and let a user edit it in the appropriate Office application while keeping the Copilot conversation going. The document can be shared with other users too, who can use the prompt Copilot to tweak it. Albeit an interesting approach, we suspect the system's reliance on OneDrive, rather than that enterprise favorite, SharePoint, might put off some customers. The new feature is also only rolling out to Frontier customers in Chat and Cowork. There's also a question-mark over Microsoft's commitment. The company is quick to drop or deprecate technology when its attention drifts elsewhere. The ability to create a theme in Outlook with Copilot is an example. Less than two years ago, Microsoft announced "Themes by Copilot in Outlook" which, according to the software and cloud biz, marked "the first instance of dynamic AI-generated theming in productivity applications." Themes by Copilot in Outlook, for users with a Copilot license, was a relatively simple piece of technology and could be dynamic, showing imagery inspired by the user's locale (if location permissions were enabled) and updating at regular intervals, for example, based on the current weather. It was all terribly exciting, and Microsoft imagined a world where users might fiddle with their productivity applications in the same way that "you might accent your desk with a candle or photos, spruce up your office with artwork or plants." After all, what's better than watching a beautiful sunset while Outlook quietly explodes in the background? However, after less than two years, the feature is for the chop, according to a post in Microsoft's Message Center. "Themes by Copilot," it wrote at the weekend, "will be removed from Settings, and users will no longer be able to select or return to a Theme by Copilot after changing to a different theme." If you're currently using a Theme by Copilot, it won't go anywhere until you change it, but after that, there's no going back. It's unclear why Microsoft is retiring the feature so soon after announcing it. It might be due to low usage (we can imagine some administrators weren't happy that users could override the selected appearance of their tools) or a step back from the Copilot All The Things approach Microsoft has taken in recent years. It is, however, a salutary warning for anyone enthusiastically embracing Office in Copilot, an interesting feature that will make for some impressive keynotes. It will also need to demonstrate its worth or face the same fate as Themes by Copilot when Microsoft moves on to The Next Big Thing. ®

articles.title: London cabbies want Sadiq Khan to slam the brakes on robotaxis
articles.text: London's minicab drivers want Mayor Sadiq Khan to put the brakes on robotaxis before they threaten thousands of jobs, with a new City Hall report casting doubt on whether the capital is ready for driverless cars. The Independent Workers' Union of Great Britain (IWGB) has called on Transport for London (TfL) to halt the rollout following the publication of a London Assembly Transport Committee report on Monday. The 66-page report makes uncomfortable reading for the companies hoping to unleash fleets of driverless taxis on London's streets. "As it stands, we currently have not heard sufficient evidence to persuade us that London should welcome autonomous passenger services," it concludes. Google's Waymo, British startup Wayve, and Chinese tech giant Baidu are among those gearing up to bring autonomous passenger services to London. Waymo has already been testing its cars in the capital and hopes to launch a commercial fleet of "low hundreds" this year, subject to regulatory approval. Uber and Wayve have secured TfL private hire licenses for vehicles offering supervised self-driving rides, meaning a human driver remains legally in control, and Freenow and Baidu are targeting a fully driverless launch in 2027. London has around 105,000 licensed private hire drivers, many of whom have reason to worry about cars that can do their jobs without them. "Every car feeds a family, and the prospect of not being able to earn money leaves us all with a deep uncertainty as to how we will provide for them. We already struggle to get by as it is," said Gholomreza "Rez" Kamyabi, an Uber driver and vice chair of the IWGB Private Hire Drivers union. The committee heard warnings that robotaxis could put large numbers of drivers out of work, and wants TfL to work with unions and operators to retrain, redeploy, and fund those affected. The IWGB, however, wants the rollout stopped. "The IWGB Private Hire Drivers Union opposes the rollout of driverless cars," said union president Alex Marshall, warning the technology could put thousands out of work while benefiting tech companies and investors. Jobs aren't the only concern. Under the government's interim Automated Passenger Services permitting scheme, the Driver and Vehicle Standards Agency (DVSA) issues operating permits. TfL must consent before a service launches in London, but cannot independently suspend or revoke a permit once issued. TfL also has no formal say over existing driverless trials, and operators aren't legally required to report incidents to it, although some have shared information voluntarily. The report details several incidents involving autonomous test vehicles, including a car reportedly entering a police crime scene cordon in April, another filmed turning the wrong way into a one-way street in June, and a reported collision with a motorcycle in July. It also questions how robotaxis would handle medical emergencies, passenger safety, and accessibility. None of the autonomous vehicles currently being trialed are wheelchair accessible. Then there's congestion. Robotaxis could lure passengers away from public transportation while adding more traffic as vehicles travel empty between fares. The committee wants operators to report their empty mileage so TfL can assess the impact. Londoners aren't exactly clamoring for the technology either. A YouGov survey commissioned by the committee found that 42 percent opposed autonomous passenger vehicles, compared with 29 percent who supported them. Just 29 percent said they would be likely to use one. The committee stopped short of calling for a ban, instead recommending tougher safety requirements, giving TfL powers to cap vehicle numbers, and a process to request the immediate suspension of permits. It also wants TfL to take over permitting when the Automated Vehicles Act is fully implemented, expected in the second half of 2027. At the time of the investigation, TfL had not yet published the criteria it would use to approve driverless passenger services. So London is preparing for robotaxis while its transport authority works out the rules, Assembly members question the benefits, and cab drivers demand the whole thing be stopped. Still, at least the cars won't complain about their working conditions.®

Mars may be a hellhole, but the moon is not far behind

The US and China are racing to build bases on the moon, with NASA hoping to establish a small lunar city by the end of the century. But the moon is a tremendously hostile place to set up camp.

A sprawling lunar base must be safe for its inhabitants, protected from falling asteroids, endless cosmic radiation, razor-sharp lunar dust, and torturous temperature swings. It also must be somewhat self-sustaining.

That will require autonomous robots, nuclear power, and a way to use the moon’s resources to keep the base operating. But the chief obstacle may be one of political will.

articles.title: Pigeon-powered internet packet goes under the hammer at Christie's
articles.text: A piece of internet history that once traveled strapped to a pigeon's leg is up for auction at Christie's, where someone has already bid $4,000 for what might be the world's most expensive ping. The unusual lot is a surviving IP packet from a 2001 experiment in which Norwegian Linux enthusiasts decided to find out whether the internet could, in fact, run on birds. The idea dates back to April 1, 1990, when American network engineer David Waitzman published RFC 1149, titled A Standard for the Transmission of IP Datagrams on Avian Carriers. Written in the wonderfully dry language of an official internet standards document, the April Fools' proposal outlined how carrier pigeons could transport IP datagrams between locations. It noted that avian carriers could provide high bandwidth, although latency would be another matter entirely. Most people appreciated the joke and moved on. The Bergen Linux User Group (BLUG), however, decided to actually build the thing. On April 28, 2001, the group put RFC 1149 to the test using racing pigeons, printers, and scanners. IP packets were printed as hexadecimal strings on strips of paper, attached to the birds' legs, and flown between two lofts 5km (roughly 3 miles) apart. The results hardly amounted to a ringing endorsement of pigeon-powered networking. Nine packets were dispatched, but only four replies came back, giving the experiment a packet-loss rate of about 56 percent. Still, the network worked, at least in the loosest possible sense of the word. Actual IP packets had traveled through the air without a single router, fiber-optic cable, or telecoms provider getting involved. One of those packets has now resurfaced at auction house Christie's as part of its Fine Printed Books & Manuscripts Including Americana and Science auction. The item is a small scroll of paper measuring just 41mm by 210mm, complete with creases from being rolled up and attached to the pigeon's leg. It is now framed, with an inscription on the reverse identifying it as the property of Waitzman, to whom it was presented in 2002. Christie's initially estimated the packet would fetch between $2,000 and $3,000, but bidding has already reached $4,000. The auction closes on October 13. The auction house describes the experiment as an example of the internet's tradition of the "artful hack," celebrating the technical ingenuity and sense of humor of its early community. There is, of course, something rather fitting about an internet packet that took to the skies 25 years ago now commanding thousands of dollars. Most packets disappear into the ether once they've served their purpose. This one ended up in a frame and is being sold by Christie's. Not bad for something delivered by a pigeon. ®
