articles.title: Imagine there's no Shiny Hunters – AI could make human hacking crews obsolete
articles.text: KETTLE The FBI has announced what appears to be a third arrest in the ShinyHunters investigation, following the group's breach of Bureau systems, even as AI advances potentially leave human hackers on borrowed time.  You can listen to the latest episode of The Kettle on this page, Spotify, Apple Podcasts, or YouTube. You can also subscribe on those platforms to be notified when a new episode goes live. A second vulnerability discovered by Anthropic's Mythos model has been exploited in the wild, and it's not one that humans probably would have discovered, begging the question just how important we are in the future of cybercrime. Join host Brandon Vigliarolo, cybersecurity editor Jessica Lyons, and senior reporter Tom Claburn to discuss those stories, and what they mean for the future of cybersecurity, on this week's episode. A lightly edited transcript is below: Brandon (00:01) Hey everyone, and welcome to the latest episode of The Register's Kettle Podcast. I'm your host, Reg reporter Brandon Vigliarolo, and this week we've got a couple cybersecurity stories to chat about, but that doesn't mean we're leaving AI out of the conversation, of course. With me to chat about some arrests and new revelations about the capabilities of Anthropic's Mythos model are Reg cybersecurity editor Jess Lyons and senior reporter Tom Claburn. Thanks to both of you for coming on. Tom (00:27) Yeah, thank you. Jessica (00:28) Good to be here. Brandon (00:29) So Jess, let's start with the FBI's continuing crusade against who seems to be its new arch nemesis, the Shiny Hunters cyber extortion crew. So as I understand, one guy was arrested at the end of last month and now they bagged another one this week. Is that right? Jessica (00:44) Well, this looks like it brings the count up to three, actually. Brandon (00:48) Right, because of today's announcement, right? [Ed: The show is recorded on Friday.] Jessica (00:50) Yes, today's announcement. The FBI director this morning put out this cryptic message on X, and then it was also emailed to news reporters saying that our agents in the field have arrested another suspected co-conspirator of the Shiny Hunters group. And this of course is related to the late September hack that stole a ton of data on agents and people who wanted to be hired by the FBI about their names, jobs, physical locations, emergency contact information. Brandon (01:23) How many people's data was stolen? I mean, it was a ton, wasn't it? Jessica (01:28) I mean, they claim it was everyone's. So is what they claimed. And sometimes these claims are inflated a bit just to increase extortion demands and hopefully get payments, but it was by all accounts a ton of information. Brandon (01:48) As Shiny Hunters told you they were doing this not for monetary gain, but literally to prove how good they were at this stuff, right? Jessica (01:55) Exactly. Right. Brandon (01:56) So there might be some inflation going on here. Who knows? Either way, it seems to have attracted the FBI's attention. Jessica (02:01) Yes for sure. So today we get this message from the director and he says that there's been another arrest. So I immediately reached out and asked the FBI, is this a third? Is this referring to some of the earlier arrests that have been reported? Because they told me earlier in the week also that we've arrested that we made, quote, multiple arrests related to this hack. So then they said we have no further comment, but the New York Times is reporting that it's a Canadian citizen who was arrested in Pennsylvania. So that would be the first arrest that happened in America if this is true. Brandon (02:41) I really don't understand why if you are a relatively high-profile cyber criminal who's going to try to attack the FBI, you would do so from within the boundaries of the country that the FBI has jurisdiction over. That to me sounds like a dumb move, right? These guys are obviously good at their craft, maybe not practical planning. I mean, honestly, I wouldn't do it if if I were in an extradition country at all. Because the other two guys were arrested where? Jessica (03:07) One was in the Netherlands and then one is reportedly detained in Jordan. Brandon (03:12) Okay, so right, both countries that I'm assuming will extradite people to the United States. Jessica (03:16) Right. Brandon (03:17) I would assume the people doing this kind of thing would be Russians, right? Whenever I hear about a cybercrime crew, I always assume it's China or Russia. That's where you're going to be safe. Jessica (03:25)  No, but that's really the interesting thing about this group is that they're English speakers. It's primarily North America, the UK, and Western Europe. And this whole move, the first thing I asked them was, "Well, how much money are you demanding?" And they immediately told me, "This is not financially motivated, this is to preserve our reputation." They wanted the FBI to walk back these earlier statements that they had made during the Instructure breach. And that affected Canvas, this educational tech platform that's used by tons of K-12 schools and universities. And so they didn't like the FBI's implication in that that they were quote unquote violent criminals, that they used intimidation tactics. It was implied that there were cases of sextortion. And so they wanted the FBI to walk this back. And I said, "Well, that's not going to happen. So doesn't this just put a huge target on your back and you already have a pretty big one?" And again, they just are determined that this is going to restore their business, show what great hackers they are, and encourage other – they call them their corporate partners, these are the extortion victims – encourage those organizations to pay these multimillion [dollar] demands when they're breached. Brandon (04:52) Right, because obviously these guys they do have an extortion business, right? That's their main thing. There is financial motivation in this, right? Jessica (04:56) Right. I mean by some accounts they are the most successful cybercrime business. They've extorted an estimated $70 million just in the last year. And they're very good at what they do. This also seems a little bit reckless even by their standards to go after the FBI. Brandon (05:23) Even if it's a politically motivated stunt or reputationally motivated, it seems like a bad idea, especially like you said, if some of them are located in the United States. But now I'm also curious, because this is a gang of clearly talented cyber criminals, but they broke into the FBI and they got a huge target painted on their back, and now we've seen allegedly three, possibly more arrests that the FBI might not be talking about. But at least three arrests of their members in the course of two weeks after they break into the FBI. Now, I imagine the FBI is probably better than a lot of people at logging things on their network, but it kind of makes me wonder, okay, they broke into the FBI and now the FBI has nabbed three of them. Could the FBI in the federal government be catching cyber criminals more easily than they do? Like they just haven't hit the wrong target. The fact that they busted into the FBI, well that let the dog off the leash. But I onder sometimes, if you're busting into Microsoft or you're stealing things from other companies, do they have better attribution and better ways of tracking these people down than they usually do? Tom (06:36) Do we know what the initial lead was that led the FBI to arrest them? And was the fact that one of them was already publicly known? Jessica (06:44) Well, see, that's the thing. And until today's arrest, both of these two were publicly known. And so my question that I've been asking a lot of security researchers, third party security researchers, because the FBI won't address any of this on the record, is just say, hey, look we got two of these criminals. So but again, they're already known. One has been arrested previously. And so those two seemed kind of like easy gets to me. I don't know what the leads were that led them to the latest arrest. And again, I haven't been able to confirm it with the FBI that this was somebody who was arrested in America and as a Canadian citizen, I'm trying to do that. But it does seem a little stunning. And the typical answers that I get is, well, there's reasons not to make arrests public sometimes, especially with this group in particular, some of them are very young. The person in Jordan, I believe, is 16 who was detained. So a lot of times you don't necessarily want to arrest somebody if they are under 18. It's better to kind of keep an eye on them. And if you can see what they're doing and who they're talking to, that can lead you to people who can be prosecuted as adults, which is typically preferable in these cases. It does seem that we could be seeing more arrests. And that's something that I am always asking the law enforcement sources that I talk to, the private resources or private company sources that I talk to. And the bottom line that they always come back to is that, well, it's more difficult than it looks. And then with Shiny Hunters, with a group like this, it's more a brand than an individual or a group of a dozen individuals or so at this point. So it's just the brand is going to continue, whether or not it's the same, you know, quote unquote leadership, maybe not, but the brand isn't really going anywhere. Brandon (08:48) So have you spoken to them since these arrests started happening? No? Jessica (08:51) No, I have not spoken to them since these arrests started happening. There's been claims that their leak site is going to be back up online shortly, but at this point that's down. The channels that I speak to them on are down. So we'll see. Tom (09:09) I wonder, has the advent of AI-driven bug hunting changed the reputation game for them? It was one thing to boast about your elite skills back when you were doing it yourself. Now that a lot of these people may or may not have access to open source models, GLM 5.3 or maybe they even have a red team account somewhere with one of the big providers, is there any sense that they should be a little bit more modest that maybe they're not doing all the work and the AI is doing it? Or are people still trying to claim all the credit for their own skills and not really disclosing, oh yeah, I had Claude do that for me. Jessica (09:46) At this point, I don't think especially with this group, I don't think it really matters because even before these AI models were really good at finding and exploiting zero days, they've been doing that for a while now. So I feel like they've already established their reputation that they are good at what they do. And then they're also really good at the social engineering part of it, which is a big piece. They're good they're good at convincing people on phone calls that they are a contractor who's locked out or they're an employee who's locked out and they need to reset their password or their MFA. So they have developed scripts and there have been indications that they're recruiting people and that they do have AI kits that can help with the social engineering piece of it now, especially. But I don't think at this point it really matters whether it was a human Shiny Hunter or whether it was a Shiny Hunter using an AI model to find a zero day and break into your organization. I don't think that matters too much to the people who are the victims who are being extorted or really for the group's reputation. Tom (10:53) So if these people are as good as they say they are, are they good enough to get sort of an out by being hired by the FBI? Isn't that kind of the traditional way? Jessica (11:00) That's right. Brandon (11:01) That's what I was thinking too, right? If you've got a 16-year-old on the hook, you can be like, "Look, you're either going to jail, we're going to keep watching you, or you're coming to work for us" kind of thing. Jessica (11:11) That definitely, I think that that would be a smart move. I mean, then you do have always the risk, like we saw with the arrest from the Dutch police. Here was somebody who was working for a private security firm after serving some time and then being quote unquote reformed. And so there's always the risk that the draw and the potential money-making opportunities from crime are a lot higher than they are working for law enforcement or working for a private company. And or even, that was a question I asked and they didn't answer. I said, "Well, you're so good at this, so why don't you use your skills for good here and not have to worry about getting arrested and constantly hiding your tracks?" And Shiny Hunters wouldn't answer that question. Brandon (12:00) I think the answer to that's pretty obvious is that there's more money if you're doing it illegally. Jessica (12:03) Right. There's a lot more money. There's like tens of millions more. Brandon (12:07) I mean the FBI would probably have to offer these kids a lot of cash, right? Why don't you come clean and be a white hat? What is it going to take for that? I mean, I guarantee it's going to be a lot of money. Jessica (12:14) Right and if they are young too, I mean, typically they don't end up serving a lot of time, if any, especially if they're teenagers or even young adults. So you spend five years in jail and then you get out and you go back to making millions doing this. Sadly the financial incentive is there to keep on working for the bad guys. Brandon (12:43) And I mean, I guess if you're good enough, that's the thing too, right? If the United States government's going to court you, it wouldn't be surprising to me if a foreign government wanted to court you as well. And basically told you, like, look, we'll give you safe haven here. You can keep doing whatever illegal shit you want as long as it's not targeting our people, right? Like target people outside the US and we don't care. Or outside Russia or China or whatever. It's really interesting to think about what thkind of careers these people could have if they decided to do things the right way or for the right people, I guess. But moving on from this gangbust to some AI enabled cybercrime as well. Mythos. There was some interesting information about Mythos's capabilities that came out this week. Jess, I think the story you wrote was talking about this is like the second vulnerability detected by Mythos that's been exploited in the wild. Is that right? Jessica (13:35) Right, that's right. That's according to a Vulnchek security researcher who's been tracking this ever since the start of Mythos partner program. And this is the second one. It was kind of interesting because it's really wonky, really nerdy from a math perspective here. It was a critical authentication bypass in Rejetto HTTP file server, HFS. And so this it essentially allowed full admin access and then remote code execution. But it's something that is it's not very likely that a human on their own would have uncovered this one. Brandon (14:17) Right. Right. So this is yeah, tell me a bit more about that. So what did it involve? It was some weird math or some weird something to do with the way a random number generator was generating random numbers, right? Jessica (14:27) Yes. Exactly. So Mythos was able, they analyzed the source code for this open source project. And then Mythos, the AI, realized that the random number generator was insecure. It could reverse this, and it also was leaking. So then it was able to reverse this, access the leak, and from that access the – Brandon (14:54) What was it leaking? Just something to do with its hash or the way it was creating numbers or? Jessica (15:00) Yes, it was leaking the output, the generator. This PRNG was leaking its output. Brandon (15:07) Okay. And then Mythos was able to basically figure out this is not as random as it's supposed to be and I can kind of reverse engineer the algorithm. Yeah. Jessica (15:11) I can reverse it. Exactly. Right. But again, it's something that would have been tricky for a human, even a human who is really good at math to spend the time doing this. So we saw a security researcher who is using with Horizon 3, they've been using Mythos ever since it was announced to pen test and find a lot of vulnerabilities. And so they were the ones who uncovered this. And then the researcher, Zach Hanley, he published this video showing how to exploit this flaw and achieve remote code execution. And then the next day, this CVE, which does have a patch too, has been updated, but the next day the CVE was already being exploited. Brandon (15:58) Ta da. Yeah, publish a proof of concept for this zero day and all of a sudden someone latches onto it. I mean, from what I was seeing, it was an IP in China, but it was very narrowly targeted, right? Like there were only a few victims. Jessica (16:11) Yes. They were targeting the US and Japan. There's only been a few so far. It picked up a bit over the weekend, but it hasn't been widely exploited. Brandon (16:26) Okay. So it's the Rejetto HTTP file server. And is that a widely deployed piece of open source software? Are there a lot of potential targets here to be exploited? Jessica (16:40) I'm honestly not quite sure how widely used it is. I don't know. Maybe Tom, do you have a better idea of that? Tom (16:46) I don't know. Is it visible in Shodan? Brandon (16:49) I'm not sure. Jessica (16:50) I believe so. Brandon (16:51) Either way, some people are finding it, right? And they're exploiting it. So hopefully people who have this running are getting it updated. But Tom, this actually kind of makes me think about a discussion I think we had maybe last week or the week before about who's liable for these sorts of things, right? This is a bug that wouldn't have probably been found by human researchers. And I'm sure there's an argument to be made for the likely wouldn't have been found part of that. But I find it interesting that this is an incredibly complicated, tiny, hard to notice bug that was found by an AI and promptly exploited. Is Anthropic on the hook at all for these discoveries being made and exploited, or do you think it's the same as any kind of proof of concept? Tom (17:31) I don't think for the discoveries, but it is sort of an interesting question because just this week they did a bunch of reorientation of their security programs. They added another tier for their defense program so you can get access to the models and they refuse a little bit less, or you can be a red team researcher and have even fewer refusals, or be at the special government level where you have almost no refusals. And so they reorganized that program and then they also opened up a critical infrastructure vulnerability program and released OSS scanner, which is a way for prominent open source projects to get free AI enabled reports about possible vulnerabilities. So to the extent that they're offering a program that purports to control these things, if it looks like they're doing a bad job and there's a bunch of stuff leaking out, then I suppose someone could bring a claim that they're negligent in the administration of these programs. They're not doing well enough. But I think just using a tool and discovering something is not going to create problems for anybody. It's going to be the application. Brandon (18:42) Did they explain why they were redoing the structure of that program at all? I'm just kind of curious what they justified that as. Tom (18:47) I assume it's for lack of participation because they had it fairly tightly tied up and I think they're trying to make it easier for people. They said that this is their desire to help and bring defenders up to speed with the tools that attackers already have. But I think it's also coming in the wake of the Hugging Face incident and all the other ones that have been disclosed, they realize that if they aren't seen being proactive, legislators are going to be pushing them harder. Not that there's been any effective legislation about AI recently, but there's going to be more pressure on that if all of a sudden people are using their stuff to break into companies and the defenders just don't have access to tools to fix it. The thing that surprised me is one of their posts they were talking about, they think in two years the defenders will have an advantage, which would be a very optimistic spin on things since the traditional security formulation is the defenders have to be right all the time and the attacker only needs to be right once. I'd be surprised if the balance of advantage tips in the favor of defenders. But there is some argument to be made that if you're writing code with a really good LLM and you have good security people who know what you're doing, you may be able to deploy with far fewer vulnerabilities than you might otherwise. There's a lot of Rust rewriting going on and that's going to help just by default for a lot of memory bugs that might exist in other languages. Does that really shift the balance of power? It's hard to say. Brandon (20:22) I don't see it either. Like you said, a defender has to be right all the time, an attacker has to be right just once. And if everyone's got an LLM that they're using to – especially if, maybe this is not really that probable because Anthropic is doing a great job of controlling access to these things, but I feel like if you're loosening the reins a little bit and giving more people access to these security models, that's going to open the door to someone misusing them too. Right? Tom (20:51) At some point, I would think that a lot of this pressure would drive more people into sort of provably secure stuff. There are methodologies for doing it, it's just that almost no one spends the money to have their software provably correct. And I think it's very difficult when you have an ecosystem with so many moving parts and dependencies than some little piece of code that's maintained by a couple people somewhere. But I think that there's probably going to be more interest in that and if they can start doing that with some of the more critical pieces of infrastructure, it'll help. Brandon (21:30) That would be anything that can give defenders a better advantage, right? AI has not made anyone feel more safe, I don't think. I don't know if I would classify it as the security nightmare that a lot of people have been saying. Jess, you follow this stuff a lot more closely than I do. What's the general consensus in the sort of defender world about AI? Are people optimistic about its capabilities? Are they worried that it's just going to make things worse? Jessica (21:58) Pretty much within the security community, it's more a sense of "it could be safe if we actually secure it and that would prevent a lot of these worst case scenarios," but that hasn't been a priority at the AI companies. So until that starts happening, then we get the AI that we deserve. So hopefully all of these recent incidents will be a little bit more motivation to do a better jobm securing AI systems, but up until now it hasn't been. And again, this is something that we've seen with pretty much any emerging technology – laptops, cloud, any emerging technology, security typically isn't the priority until bad things start happening. And then there's the call to do a better job securing them. At that point it's a little bit late in the game, but hopefully it happens. Brandon (22:50) Security isn't what makes these companies with this new emerging tech money, right? It's the afterthought of well we'll get the really cool things out there first and then we'll worry about protecting them later on. Jessica (22:56) Right. Yep. And then we'll secure it. Right. Brandon (23:04) Once you've got cancer, then we'll cure it. We won't worry about trying to prevent it from happening. It's an interesting world we live in, and it's only being made more interesting by all this AI. And you know what, chances are it's going to keep being interesting. We can't even get away from it on a week we're talking about security, of course. So, you know, hey, tune in to future episodes when I'm sure we'll have more interesting stuff about AI to share. ®

articles.title: When you just need to build a tiny desktop app: TinyJS
articles.text: As the world’s billionaires anxiously plot datacenters to run trillions of lines of AI-generated slop code, one software engineer has zagged in a completely different direction: building an ecosystem for writing and running small apps that run on desktop computers, like it was 1992 all over again. Self-described “maker of things” Tarwin Stroh-Spijer has created a JavaScript runtime, called TinyJS, for making very small applications (many occupying ~6MB or less on disk) for macOS, Linux or Windows. To be clear, TinyJS is not a “no code” framework with hobbled capabilities. It offers the full programming power of JavaScript, along with the visual rendering and communication capabilities of the underlying OS. The trick to TinyJS’s frugality is that it uses the WebView window of each OS, utilizing the built-in browser engine to visually render the app, rather than implementing a UI layer from scratch. It uses WebKit to run apps in this fashion on macOS, WebView2 for Windows, and WebKitGTK for Linux. TinyJS’s approach is starkly different from using the Electron framework, which bundles a Chromium open source browser core with each desktop app. But whereas Electron promises an identical look-and-feel of an app across all platforms, TinyJS apps will have slight visual variances when run on the different platforms, owing to minor differences in how each OS’s rendering engine works. The Electron app pays for this cross-platform uniformity: with Electron, even the most basic application can weigh 150MB. Rust is not always the answer The core of TinyJS is txiki.js, an ultra-compact JavaScript runtime written by Saúl Ibarra Corretgé that makes Deno and Bun look like behemoths. The starter package is about 5.6MB and the launcher takes up another megabyte or so. The rest of the package is all developer code, basically. Stroh-Spijer also simplified the development process by using the OS’ interprocess communication mechanisms for handling data transfer, eliminating the need to bundle an HTTP server for each app, along with all the security headaches that entails. All coding in TinyJS is done in JavaScript, CSS and HTML – no compiling necessary. There’s plenty of room for creativity here, as web design capabilities have been growing by leaps and bounds of late. The Tauri project has a similar aim of creating the tiny apps, and can deliver a desktop app in 10MB, but that framework has some drawbacks, Stroh-Spijer noted on the TinyJS website. The main one is that you have to write applications in Rust – which requires learning Rust, among other drawbacks. Also, TinyJS hands over a lot of the app’s substrate to the OS – such as dialogs, menus, tray, clipboard, auto-updates – that with Tauri would have to be imported one plugin at a time. Developers don’t need Node.js as a dependency here, unless they want to run a framework that requires it, such as Vite. It can also support other JavaScript frameworks like React, Vue, and Svelte. Or it can run with no dependencies at all. You can also use TinyJS to wrap a Webpage, by pointing the window to a URL. Imagine having your favourite site as an app on your desktop. A shelf of diminutive apps With TinyJS, Stroh-Spijer created an “app store” that can be run, natch, from the desktop (the zipped Windows version can be downloaded here). As of press time, it indexes 25 sample apps he wrote. The example apps, all free, vary in utility and whimsy. The shelf includes a world clock (which ships as a 3.8MB zip file), a clipboard history app (3.7MB), a markdown editor (4.9MB), a desktop ghost (3.8MB), a SQLite browser (4.1MB) and, most impressively, a clone of the iconic Winamp music player, which demands only 7.4MB from your hard drive. Once you convince Windows Defender to trust the launcher, you can download and open the app of your choice directly from the shelf. In my tests, the copy-and-paste app, clearly written for Mac hotkeys, was still too buggy for Windows, though the world clock ran just fine and consumed only 15.5MB of RAM on my box. (Caveat emptor: the launcher checks the hash to ensure the validity of downloaded apps, though you’re trusting that Stroh-Spijer harbors no evil intent here). Or, just skip the examples and build your own test apps. Today’s personal computers are powerful, but there are still many good reasons for building apps that would be petite even by last century's standards. Commercial applications (those still around anyway) and Web browsers are voracious RAM consumers, so adding more tools to the desktop with little overhead is a positive. Plus, unlike the bloaty apps, minuscule apps start fast, and, in theory, draw less power on laptops. And just like the TikTok meme of the woman who insists on bringing her dog on the plane because it’s just “a tiny dog,” users may want to add these apps to their desktops, because, well, they’re tiny. ®

articles.title: Mars may be a hellhole, but the moon is not far behind
articles.text:
Welcome to the second space race. You can be forgiven for experiencing déjà vu. Last time, it was the Soviet Union and the United States vying to be the first to plant some flags. Now it’s a sprint to the lunar surface between America and China—alongside a host of varyingly friendly and rival nations—plus a cornucopia of private spaceflight companies. And this time it looks like they’re getting ready to set up camp. There will be, the contenders say, bases on the moon, permanently inhabited castles under the stars.

The notion of a moon base, fanciful as it might sound, isn’t new. But this year, under the leadership of Administrator Jared Isaacman, NASA has been flooding the zone with bold announcements. If all goes according to plan—a plan that will likely cost tens of billions of dollars to start—there will be drones, robotic landers, communication satellites, and a nuclear power plant; there will be plant terrariums and moonquake sensors; there will be mechanized scouts exploring craters for water.

Initial astronaut missions to the lunar surface, which the US is currently planning to start in 2028, will be focused on exploration and technological experimentation. But the idea is that we will—some time in the 2030s—get to a point where there will be habitation quarters for long-term stays, surrounded by a network of scientific research stations, resource mining and processing plants, and landing pads for spaceships. “It’s going to be an expanse,” says Carlos García-Galán, NASA’s moon base program manager—one that will add up to “hundreds of square miles.”

The effort is undoubtedly being fueled by nationalistic competition. China has near-identical plans to build its own base on the moon. And being first matters, because the “victor” gets to define the terms. What is the moon, exactly? Is it a militarized outpost? Is it a manufacturing hub? Is it a wilderness to be studied and preserved?

But there are also other reasons to go. Earth’s companion contains primeval rocks that hold clues to the formation of the entire solar system. The lunar surface, with virtually no atmosphere in the way, is an ideal place to put telescopes that could examine the most ancient epochs of the cosmos. The far side of the moon would be “a fantastic place to explore the further universe,” says Josef Aschbacher, the European Space Agency’s director general. And it’s way more energy efficient to launch rockets from the low-gravity lunar surface than it is from Earth, meaning sending astronauts—or robotic spacecraft—farther into the solar system will become much less difficult. “The moon is critical. It will be a stepping stone for going further—that means to Mars and beyond,” says Aschbacher.

But if these bold visions are to become reality, there’s a daunting amount of work to be done. A sprawling moon base must be safe for its astronaut inhabitants—protected from falling asteroids, endless cosmic radiation, razor-sharp lunar dust, and torturous temperature swings. It also must be somewhat self-sustaining, so that it can weather changing political fortunes and not cost ruinous amounts of money to maintain. For that, we’ll need to find a way to use the moon’s resources to keep the base operating—and ideally generating revenue. And we’ll need autonomous robots that can build, maintain, and expand the base even when their human masters aren’t present. “It’s almost like starting civilization from scratch,” says Simon Middleburgh, co-director of the Nuclear Futures Institute at Bangor University in Wales.

Assuming we can overcome these starting challenges, decades from now—let’s say, by the year 2100—our initial moon bases could grow from barely visible structures into luminous cities, perhaps not too dissimilar from those dreamed up by authors and screenwriters the world over. “It’s like science fiction today that we really want to turn into a reality,” says García-Galán. Will anyone succeed?

The moon is a tremendously hostile place to set up camp. In general, daytime temperatures can reach more than 250 °F; at night, they can plummet to less than –200 °F. Exposed to the vacuum of space, the surface is constantly showered in carcinogenic radiation and frequently hit by meteoroids. And its volcanic dust is sticky and corrosive, a destroyer of equipment and choker of lungs. 

Sadly, the lunar south pole—the area NASA is targeting—is even harsher. NASA wants to build a base there because its permanently shadowed craters are thought to harbor caches of water ice, which would be more precious than gold. Purify it, and you can water crops and hydrate astronauts; split it into oxygen and hydrogen, and you have breathable air and rocket propellant. But the temperature in those craters can be lower than –410 °F, making them some of the coldest places in the known universe. On the surface outside those pits, astronauts would be bathed in the scorching sun for 14 days before experiencing an equally long frigid night.

But there is only so much money we can spend on safety. “What it comes down to is acceptable risk of death,” Philip Metzger, a spaceflight engineering researcher at the Florida Space Institute, said while pondering some of the dangers. “What can we reasonably survive without breaking the bank?”

Temperature is one of the easiest problems to handle. Materials science has come a long way, and there are myriad metals, ceramics, plastics, compounds, and alloys that can resist wild temperature swings. Radiators keep things cool; heaters keep batteries from dying prematurely. Astronauts survive just fine too, with their fancy spacesuits—but that technology has proved itself only during brief excursions. It’s not yet clear how long this equipment could operate under such tempestuous conditions.

The temperature in the moon’s south pole craters can be lower than –410 °F, making them some of the coldest places in the known universe.

Outside those pits, astronauts would be bathed in the scorching sun for 14 days before experiencing an equally long frigid night.

Space radiation, which can wreak havoc on electronics and trigger a cancerous division of cells, is far more pernicious. And as Stuart George, a physicist at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston, explains, it comes in two unpleasant forms. 

The first is galactic cosmic rays, which rain down on the moon almost constantly. “They’re made by supernovas and neutron star mergers—all these kinds of things,” says George. And because the atomic nuclei, protons, and electrons that make them up are moving at significant fractions of the speed of light, these cosmic rays have oodles of kinetic energy, meaning they can punch through thin shielding (say, a metal wall) with ease. “They also have this habit where the heavier ions are fragmenting in that shielding and making secondary particles,” says George. That means if your shield is too thin, the astronauts behind it will be blasted with a surprisingly large dose of radiation. 

Then you have the sun. It may sustain life on Earth, but without our planet’s thick atmosphere and magnetic bubble to get in its way, moonwalkers will occasionally be blasted by one of its paroxysms: a solar flare (a burst of diverse types of radiation) or a coronal mass ejection (volleys of magnetized plasma). “During Apollo, they knew that if a large solar flare occurred while the crew was on the moon, there would be no way to keep them alive,” says Metzger. The crew could have developed acute radiation sickness and perished in a matter of days.

The way to survive a powerful solar flare or coronal mass ejection is straightforward: “Get back inside a habitat where there’s more shielding,” says George—preferably a dedicated, highly shielded “storm shelter,” essentially a thick-walled bunker. The issue is that astronauts might be outside the base, driving a rover many miles away. Coronal mass ejections take hours to days to reach the vicinity of the Earth-moon system, but solar flares can do so in under an hour. And scientists can’t yet model the sun well enough to give much advance notice. “All of the capability to forecast solar storms is kind of like where weather forecasting [was] … in the ’50s and ’60s,” says George.

As for those punchy galactic cosmic rays, the only way to avoid them would be to put a lot of stuff—lunar rocks, possibly—between the astronauts and the sky. “Build habitat modules underground,” says Chris Dreyer, director of engineering at the Center for Space Resources at the Colorado School of Mines. One option: Burrow living quarters into lava tubes, the naturally hollowed-­out volcanic tunnels created by molten rock eons ago. At this point, NASA hasn’t mentioned any plans to make its moon base subterranean, but it may need to if it wants to end up with a small lunar city.

Radiation limits the time astronauts can spend on the lunar surface over their entire life—it can total around two years max, experts estimate, before the health risk becomes too high. Unfortunately, that’s not all space will throw at them. When the Artemis II astronauts swung around the far side of the moon earlier this year, they saw curious flashes light up the silvery land below. These were the explosive deaths of small meteoroids punching into the lunar surface.

Earth is naturally protected from smaller space rocks, up to around 50 feet in diameter: They burn up inconsequentially in the atmosphere. “You don’t have that option on the moon,” says Philip Lubin, a physicist and planetary defense researcher at the University of California, Santa Barbara. Since smaller rocks plunge toward planets and moons far more frequently than larger ones do, this means the moon is often peppered by what are effectively tiny space bullets. They could easily puncture a spacesuit or the engine of a moon rover.

How do you protect astronauts from the onslaught? “The simplest answer is burial,” says Nicholas Schmerr, a planetary seismologist at the University of Maryland—conveniently, the same way you’d deal with radiation exposure. Pile up moon rocks onto your base walls or put habitable structures in lava tubes. 

Inconveniently, there’s always a chance that a bigger asteroid will come along. Even buried habitation modules would have trouble surviving an assault from a 50-footer—about the length of a semi-trailer. 

That doesn’t mean a moon base would be helpless against bigger asteroids. Planetary defense has come a long way in just a few decades. NASA’s DART mission demonstrated that it could deflect an asteroid by ramming into the rock with an uncrewed spacecraft, and cutting-­edge experiments at clandestine labs around the US suggest that a nuclear bomb could swat away or entirely vaporize errant space rocks. An array of both ground-based and space-based telescopes specifically designed to spy killers—such as the ATLAS quartet of largely automated telescopes, and the soon-to-be-launched NEO Surveyor infrared telescope—are also aiming to find 90% of the near-Earth asteroids potentially capable of wiping out entire cities (those 460 feet across) in the coming years.

All these protections apply to the moon. But asteroids 50 feet across are so stealthy that even NASA’s best telescopes would struggle to see them years or even months in advance. Odds are that they would first be seen not long before they were due to hit the lunar surface. Then what?

It’s not unreasonable to imagine several turret-like launch sites on the moon that, owing to the lower gravity and airless environment, could rapidly fire projectiles toward an incoming asteroid. Hit it hard enough and it would break into fragments. Just make sure you shoot when it is as far away as possible: “If you were to break something up into a thousand pieces, then you have a thousand impacts on the moon,” says Lubin. “That might be worse than letting it hit one place.” 

Having your base destroyed by an asteroid would be awful. But a moon base is far more likely to be imperiled by dust—which, unlike asteroids, is everywhere, all the time.

Volcanic lunar rocks, when broken down, turn into sharp, electrostatically charged, adhesive, acrid, abrasive particles. While on the moon, Apollo astronauts who inhaled some of this dust occasionally suffered from a strange “lunar hay fever,” which irritated their eyes and agitated their lungs. That same dust ate through all kinds of gear with disturbing ease. “It rips up seals, gears, motors, spacesuits, habitats—everything else it comes into contact with,” says Justin Cyrus, the CEO of Lunar Outpost, a spaceflight technology company that is providing NASA with one of the Artemis program’s moon rovers.

NASA has already developed a defense against these dark shards: the electrodynamic dust shield, or EDS. The lightweight electrodes that make up this shield—which can be layered on machinery, walls, and perhaps even spacesuits—use opposing currents to blast away the electrically charged dust. The EDS worked wonders when tested in labs on Earth, and it also demonstrated its anti-dust magic when sent to the lunar surface in 2025 as part of a NASA-sponsored robotic mission. 

Amy Fritz, a dust-mitigation researcher at Johnson Space Center, says that the EDS will likely be widely featured all over a lunar habitat. But other dust-fighting instruments are being developed too—including a lint-roller-type object inspired by gecko skin and a sci-fi-esque blaster that uses ionized nitrogen gas. Its first spray will neutralize the charge of the dust to remove its stickiness; then a second burst will clear it off the surface.

Irritatingly, the busier a base gets, the dustier things will become. As it expands to the size of a small city, rocket ships will need to deliver cargo and crew to the lunar surface on a frequent cadence. Each takeoff and landing will launch a salvo of dust in every direction, inundating the base’s infrastructure. “You have to worry about essentially being sandblasted every time,” says Fritz. 

Metzger calculates that even with landing pads more than 3,000 feet away from a base, just 10 to 20 liftoffs or landings would be sufficient to severely damage things like protective coatings on exterior walls and communications equipment. After a while, he says, “everything breaks.” 

Even if the moon base of the future is buried partly below ground, barricaded against micrometeorites and space radiation, and well equipped with dust-repelling technologies, it’s still a risky gig for any astronaut. Skipping around in a preternaturally agile way at one-sixth of Earth’s gravity will be entertaining. But “microgravity is not good for the human body,” says Dreyer. Muscle wastage, cardiovascular troubles, respiratory problems, and immune deficiencies can arise. 

Radiation, too, may always afflict lunar residents. And there’s also evidence that disease-causing microbes could stealthily sneak aboard spacecraft, even after stringent sterilization procedures. Those microbes may behave differently than they do on Earth; microgravity experiments (both real and simulated) have suggested that some become more aggressive and more likely to cause disease. “We call them the invisible crew,” says Lisa Carnell, the director of NASA’s Biological and Physical Sciences Division.

Hoping to find a better way to protect astronauts, Carnell spearheaded an experiment called AVATAR (A Virtual Astronaut Tissue Analog Response), which launched aboard the Artemis II mission. It used thumb-drive-size chips, containing cells taken from the heart, lungs, or other parts of the body, that could be switched on to act like miniature organs. Scientists have previously used this organ-on-a-chip technology for purposes like testing out new pharmaceuticals in a highly controlled setting. For Artemis II, Carnell’s crew sent up chips containing bone marrow samples taken from the mission’s four astronauts. Bone marrow makes red and white blood cells, as well as platelets—the sort of stuff that affects almost the entire human body. So seeing how space radiation and microgravity affect it would give Carnell and her team vital insight into how astronauts’ biology might change on the moon.

The advantage of organ chips is that you can make them for any astronaut and then send them into space ahead of time to see how that person’s organs will react to spaceflight. Researchers envision that data from such chips will be able to clue medics in to the specific preventive treatments or pharmaceuticals that will help moonbound astronauts on their journey.

What is NASA likely to send up sooner rather than later? “Brain organoids,” says Carnell. Yes, she adds—that sounds super weird. But it would be good to know how a real brain might respond to being on the moon for several months before people start living there.

Okay. Your vast moon base and its inhabitants are protected—as much as is possible—from the treacherous lunar environment. But astronauts’ time is extremely valuable, and humans are fragile creatures. You can’t make them do all the heavy lifting, which means that whether you’re trying to make a tiny lunar outpost or a small city, you’re going to need a lot of robots. “The buildup of the moon base, in the first years, will pretty much 99% be robotic,” says NASA’s García-Galán.

Autonomy will be there right from the start. NASA’s new version of the moon buggy, its Lunar Terrain Vehicle, can be driven by the astronauts riding in it but can also be piloted remotely from Earth (or from elsewhere on the moon). There are visions, too, of adding modular robotic arms, towing vehicles, and cargo movers—all still in the preliminary stages of planning.

Over the next few decades, though, we’ll likely want an army of robots to do our bidding: excavators to dig up lunar rocks that could be turned into concrete and bricks, plus other robots to flatten surfaces, dig trenches, create building foundations, pave landing pads, and build up dust-deflecting berms to keep the base from being sandblasted by launches and landings. Even solar panels and wiring can potentially be made from moon rocks—something that the spaceflight company Blue Origin demonstrated in labs on Earth in 2023 using a geologic simulant designed to match the composition of lunar regolith. 

Powering this robot army will require considerable energy. Two-week-long nights make solar power an impractical solution. Aside from a cornucopia of high-­capacity, extreme-temperature-resistant batteries, nuclear power is probably the only viable option. A small, car-size nuclear reactor, filled with an almost literal handful of uranium, could power a small village for a decade without needing to be refueled. And although nobody’s yet tested a nuclear reactor on the moon, few doubt that NASA and the US Department of Energy can conjure up a working design—one that perhaps wouldn’t be too different from those aboard nuclear submarines. A moon base in 2100 would probably feature multiple small, autonomously or remotely operated nuclear reactors, which—conveniently—the base-expanding robots could simply plug themselves into to recharge. 

But the biggest lunar question mark might be water, which planners want to support the astronauts—and to make fuel to launch things from the lunar surface. A process known as electrolysis, which uses electricity to snap apart molecular bonds, can be used to split water into oxygen and hydrogen, both of which could be used to make rocket fuel. Getting them this way could be far less expensive than sending either all the way from Earth. And as an added bonus, it would provide a source of breathable oxygen. 

Orbital data has revealed that there is some amount of water preserved in patches on the lunar south pole, but little is known about how much there actually is, what form it takes, or how easy it will be to extract. Will there be solid sheets of ice here and there, ready for us to excavate? Or will there be scattered ice crystals intermingled among the rocky grains, requiring some more inventive form of extraction?

A lot of the moon’s water is thought to be hiding in deep, dark craters on the south pole, where the environment is so extreme that robots may freeze up, tumble over, or lose contact with the base. “To me, that is the biggest hurdle,” says Paul van Susante, principal investigator of the Planetary Surface Technology Development Lab at Michigan Technological University.

Van Susante’s lab has been putting various construction robots through their paces in moon-like vacuum chambers filled with moon-like rocks. His team was part of NASA’s recent Break the Ice challenge, which invited engineers to build robots to test different ways to excavate such rocks. Some teams used an electric jackhammer and a scoop, while others used scrapers to peel off layers of the ground. The teams simulated the moon’s weak gravity using a crane to lift and offset the weight of the robots. Progress in this regard is speeding along. “I won’t say that’s solved, but we’ve got a lot of the puzzle pieces,” says van Susante.

Mining the water will be just one part of an extensive operation. “When you extract it, it’s not going to be clean. It needs to be purified,” says Jessica Atkin, a space botanist at Texas A&M. The technology to do this already exists and works fine on terra firma. But things in space never go the way you expect. “There’s a water purification system on the International Space Station (ISS), and it is known for getting contaminated with microbes,” she says.

But if you purify the water sufficiently—something that can handily be achieved on Earth but may falter in microgravity, where fluids flow in stranger ways—then your moon base can hit its stride. With an effective water recycling system, an increasingly populous base will never go thirsty—and, just maybe, you’ll have a lunar greenhouse. Several edible plants have been successfully grown aboard the ISS, including lettuce, mustard greens, tomatoes, and peppers. Lunar dust unfortunately makes for a terrible garden: It’s filled with far too much aluminum—and it forms a resistant layer when watered. But Atkin has shown that with the help of fertilizing fungi, chickpeas can grow in soil much like the volcanic stuff found on the moon.

Moon base inhabitants of 2100 would be supported largely by prepacked meals sent from Earth. But in time, they would start growing some of their own produce—probably with a good deal of automation for lighting, watering, and maintenance of humidity and other environmental conditions. Aside from chickpeas, there might also be plenty of lunar tomatoes. They’d be desirable not least because they’ve been bioengineered to produce higher levels of compounds called anthocyanins that, according to some studies, might help humans mitigate the cellular damage caused by space radiation.

A garden on the moon would do more than just provide food, as recent experiences on the ISS suggest. Carnell says that NASA recently caught the astronauts aboard the space station doing something sneaky. All plants up there are supposed to be confined to their growth chambers. But “we learned that the crew were pirating our leftover soil and bringing their seeds and planting their own little gardens, if you will, and hiding them in their own cabins,” she says. 

Conversations were had in the summer of 2026, after which NASA decided to let astronauts grow their own mini-gardens anywhere they wanted. “Some of the astronauts said they thrived better,” says Carnell. Nature, and gardening, has a hugely beneficial psychological effect on those kept in confined quarters hanging above Earth. That will be even truer for those living in lava tunnels under the lunar surface. “That human element is so important,” she says.

Nobody is deluded into thinking there isn’t a mountain of technological challenges in the way. Mars may be a hellhole, as the writer Shannon Stirone put it in 2021 in The Atlantic, but the moon isn’t too far behind. It’s an almost comically menacing place to be. Much about it stands in the way of building a safe, self-sustaining, robotically managed base. 

NASA wants to put the first nuclear reactor on the moon by 2030. China, partnering with Russia, wants to place its own nuclear power plant up there around 2035.

Beyond the first basic habitation module, it will take decades of experimentation and iteration on the lunar surface to get to a working moon base spanning hundreds of square miles. But few doubt that with enough time and tinkering, humanity can prevail. “It’s not an unsolvable problem,” says the University of Maryland’s Schmerr.

The chief obstacle, especially in the initial stages of building, may be one of political will. NASA is currently bringing every resource to bear on the project—something that the agency hopes could culminate in a small lunar city by the century’s end. But will that commitment continue over multiple US administrations? Will the international community also throw its weight behind the NASA-led effort? NASA has “a very ambitious plan,” says Yuqi Qian, a lunar geologist at the University of Hong Kong. “We need to keep an eye on it.” In fact, he says, “the current plan looks over-ambitious.” The agency, for example, wants to put the first nuclear reactor on the moon by 2030. (China, partnering with Russia, wants to place its own nuclear power plant up there around 2035.) 

“These sorts of projects—although very exciting, and potentially transformative for humankind—are the first ones to be delayed or scrapped,” says Middleburgh of the Nuclear Futures Institute. NASA’s direction tends to change when a new administration comes into power—sometimes dramatically so.

But several experts outside of NASA agree that, at least for now, there is definite momentum and political will behind the moon base. “NASA has very clearly expressed where they want to go, what their priorities [are], what their ambition is, and how they want to do it,” says ESA’s Aschbacher. “It was quite impressive to see.”

Even if the political will behind the US-led endeavor is maintained over the coming decades, expanding anywhere beyond an initial, compact moon base will require more than government funding. “There has to be a lunar economy for this to be self-sustaining,” says Dreyer, the space resources expert. Perhaps that will come from the production of rocket fuel, or from the mining of valuable materials on the moon that can replace similar, polluting activities on Earth. But it’s not at all clear how valuable, or not, a lunar economy will be. 

Even Isaacman, NASA’s chief, doesn’t think the moon will be a major moneymaker. “I don’t know of anything on the moon right now that’s going to be easier and more affordable to mine, manufacture, and then bring back to Earth than what we could make here on Earth,” he remarked back in February. (Instead, he suspects, mining metals from asteroids will be the path to prosperity.) 

What if, instead, a moon base earns the right to exist because it’s a place for novel scientific research? Aschbacher imagines it will be like humanity’s outposts in Antarctica. Down there, in what truly feels like another world, scientist-explorers work in a land of gleaming and endless ice to learn more about our planet’s climate, its deep past, and its resilient life-forms. “We understand planet Earth by looking into those remote places,” he says. The moon offers a similar opportunity. What discoveries await astronauts in those primordial lava tubes? What will lunar astronomers see in the night sky—with effectively no atmosphere or light pollution in the way—that those on Earth can’t?

As in all spaceflight programs, technologies developed up there will no doubt be tweaked to be used back on Earth. And a base on the moon will make exploring the rest of the solar system easier. Technologically, physiologically, and psychologically, the moon “is a proving ground for the technologies we need for Mars,” says NASA’s García-Galán.

If we play the US-China race forward, perhaps the lunar south pole of 2100 will feature several sprawling bases operated by multiple geopolitical rivals. Perhaps it’ll be an off-world powder keg of militarized territorial ambitions and jingoism. But maybe it could instead become an international cathedral to science—and the ultimate adventure destination. “Even if countries on planet Earth have difficulty talking to each other,” says Aschbacher, they might behave differently when it comes to the moon. “I’m pretty sure they will get together and see what we can do together, and see what problems we can solve.” After all, he says, up there, far from home, “you’re so dependent on each other.” 

Robin George Andrews is an award-winning science journalist and doctor of volcanoes based in London. He regularly writes about the Earth, space, and planetary sciences and is the author of two critically acclaimed books: Super Volcanoes (2021) and How to Kill an Asteroid (2024).

articles.title: Celebrating the brilliant pragmatism of TCP/IP, the wiring of the world
articles.text: It's 1988. Windows 2.0 is a DOS shell that runs on a dual-floppy 8086 PC. VGA is the aspirational video standard. A three-man startup in East London has decided to create low-cost LANs. There's not much of that and not much by way of standards, which is why a young programmer is rather excited by an emerging contender called TCP/IP. He's particularly keen because he's just finished implementing IBM's PC networking API, NetBIOS, which hurt almost as much as integrating any sort of networking with DOS. Research means library books, magazine articles, and asking questions on Usenet over kilobit dial-up. Getting the wrong idea is easy. Trying to build the TCP/IP stack on the ISO/OSI seven-layer model produces more pain, but sanity prevails, and after a bit, there's a working network. Nearly 40 years later, the once-young programmer is now a curmudgeonly Reg columnist. Floppies have become terabyte thumb drives. Kilobit modems are gigabit fiber and Wi-Fi. Graphics have come on a bit too. And he hasn't touched Windows or an Intel CPU in years. It is a transformed world. Except for one thing – everything talks to everything over TCP/IP. It's time to celebrate the digital oxygen of the global data ecosystem. TCP/IP is still newsworthy. Any apparent attempt to replace part of it is worth reporting, in this case a congestion-easing protocol called Homa superseding TCP. Only it's not a replacement, just an alternative designed to run alongside. That this is possible is due to one of the genius decisions made as TCP/IP evolved – splitting what was one protocol into two: TCP and IP. IP, the Internet Protocol, just sends packets between two addresses, best effort, no guarantees when, in what order, or even if they'll get through. The Transmission Control Protocol uses IP but delivers a reliable, ordered stream of bytes, arranging retransmission of missing data. Thus, if you don't like how TCP does things, you can add your own IP-speaking protocol to run alongside. This approach also saw TCP/IP vanquish rival protocols from very large industry incumbents, such as IBM's Systems Network Architecture (SNA) and ATM – Asynchronous Transfer Mode – from the telecoms side. Packet-switched IP can't possibly succeed, they said, with its non-deterministic transmissions of unknown latency. Nothing reliable could be built on that. TCP/IP, being open, flexible, and built by consensus by individual, inspired engineers, just got on with being useful. That had been proved on January 1, 1983, when ARPANET – the proto internet – dropped the proto when it switched over wholesale from its own NCP to TCP/IP. Known as flag days, such events weren't uncommon as previously isolated early networks had to adapt or die to the new interconnected world. TCP/IP was explicitly designed to inter-network, from the seminal paper [PDF] in 1974 by Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn. From that 13-page paper to adoption across ARPANET took nine years. Five years later, a greenhorn coder could build the stack for completely novel hardware in three months. It took longer to work out how to build an installable driver for IBM's PS/2 Micro Channel Architecture. The future wasn't hard to see. Once it had beaten the opposition, the extremely practical, extremely open soul of TCP/IP repeatedly saved it from its biggest enemy. Itself. It turned out that once we had a technology that could freely connect any number of devices to each other, end to end, we wanted to do that very much. The internet, freed of central control and gatekeepers, grew exponentially, especially after another protocol, HTTP, shyly perched on top of TCP. Naysayers predicted letting ordinary people use this would clog the internet, to the point that the introduction of image tags was seen as portending the End Times. Congestion collapse could close it all down. Fortunately, shortly before Tim Berners-Lee began work on the Web, a 1988 paper by Van Jacobson and Mike Karels, Congestion Avoidance and Control [PDF], came up with a set of strategies and tweaks to TCP that has kept the problem at bay ever since. A global network with no central control that can fix show-stopping, scale-related problems on the fly is a true wonder. Similarly, IPv4's 32-bit address field with 4.3 billion addresses seemed an over-provision, until suddenly it was nowhere near enough. A new version of IP, IPv6, was introduced in 1995 with addresses as plentiful as grains of sand in the Sahara. The trouble was that if you've got billions of devices, you can't do a flag day. IPv6 proved great for infrastructure, but not the edge. Fortunately, a router kludge called Network Address Translation (NAT) appeared, again at roughly the same time. It broke the end-to-end principle only a little bit, but let the old version of IP, IPv4, run untouched. Let's be frank. It's fugly. But it let many devices share a single public IP address, which is why everything that comes out of the box for normies still rocks IPv4 like it's 1981. Just don't ask what happened to IPv5. There are thousands of ways TCP/IP has evolved, many tiny and a few deeply silly, like RFC 1149 (IP over Avian Carriers), material relating to which is, at the time of writing, up for auction at Christie's. At heart, it is one of mankind's most brilliant technical achievements, the underpinning of everything the connected world can do, built from intelligence, vision, openness, iteration, freedom of thought, freedom of action, a rough consensus and running code. It deserves its own universal day of celebration. Let's make it January 1. Let's call it Flag Day. ®

articles.title: The ecologist revealing the invisible networks that revive rainforests
articles.text:
In a research station in central Panama, you can walk through a century of forest time, watching scrubby plots of adolescent trees give way to cathedral-­like canopies of mature growth. Forest ecologist Daisy Dent, a senior scientist at ETH Zurich, oversees this sequence of plots across the Barro Colorado Nature Monument, some of which date as far back as the 19th century. Not one of the trees she surveys was planted by human hands. She maps, measures, and tracks each trunk that emerges, revealing how waves of tree life rise from bare earth. 

Tropical forests like these are our planet’s biggest terrestrial carbon sink, accounting for around 40% of carbon stored on land. As part of an international network of researchers, Dent is deciphering the networks of animal and plant interactions that enable some forests to recover after destruction. The goal is a low-cost, high-impact alternative to typical carbon-­crediting schemes, which plant huge areas with a single species of tree. For over a decade, her research has built a body of evidence that such large “monocrop” programs could be expensive mistakes—and that more resilient forests can rebound naturally in just a few decades, re-creating ecosystems that suck up vast quantities of carbon dioxide. 

Few places are better to demonstrate this than Barro Colorado, a reserve covering the forested peninsulas and islands that formed when construction of the Panama Canal flooded the area in 1914. Under the management of the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute, generations of ecologists have amassed more than a century of records. 

That means Dent can trace why some plots rebound after clear-cutting for farming and forestry while others falter. Fruit-eating animals—including spider monkeys, bats, and parrots—are responsible for planting more than 70% of trees in tropical forests, and Dent’s dataset can tell which built each patch of trees by depositing seeds in their nutrient-rich droppings. Many of these creatures worked together to plant a diverse 70-year-old patch whose canopy is approaching the stunning structure and richness of an ancient jungle. In contrast, a patch of similar age populated by narrow trunks of a single long-lived species, Gustavia superba, hints that tropical rodents called agoutis are more or less the sole animal architects behind this more homogeneous forest. 

The data she collects helps write a playbook for when to let ecosystems regenerate and when to give them a helping hand. One 2024 estimate in Nature found that some 215 million hectares of forest worldwide (an area larger than Mexico) could regenerate naturally. “Tropical forests are underpinned by this massive network of interactions,” Dent says—interactions between life-forms like the fungi that help trees take up nutrients, as well as pollinators and seed-distributors. Supporting those relationships is key to growing forests that lock up carbon and help sustain local communities and wildlife. 

Filling in the gaps

Just over a decade ago, as the landmark Paris Agreement was being codified in 2015, forest recovery seized global attention as a solution to the climate crisis. Global leaders rallied behind plans to regrow a trillion trees, after the ecologist Thomas Crowther highlighted their potential to capture a decade’s worth of global carbon emissions. But the biggest question has lingered: How, exactly, do you regrow two trees for every star in the Milky Way?

While startups have proposed seed-spraying drones and nutrient-coated seed bombs, Dent has spent two decades studying what happens when we let forests rebuild themselves. As a PhD student around the turn of the millennium, she researched old-growth forests in northern Borneo but felt hopeless watching entire landscapes felled for palm oil plantations. Rather than despair, she turned to restoration. Then, as a postdoc in 2005, she joined Panama’s Prorena, a joint initiative between the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute and the Yale School of Forestry and Environmental Studies, which aimed at determining how best to establish diverse native forests on clear-cut land.

Back then, secondary forests—ones that grow naturally after the original forest was lost—had been “a bit of a niche research area,” Dent says. But as farming and human infrastructure have driven deforestation, resurgent forests now account for some 70% of all tropical canopies. Prorena initially followed the usual playbook of transplanting nursery trees to rangelands, but Dent began to question whether planting was necessary. In 2009, she published an encouraging paper showing that animal populations rebound quickly as forests naturally regrow.

In 2010, she began working in Barro Colorado on the plots established by the pioneering American ecologist Julie Denslow. In 1994, Denslow identified plots that had been regenerating naturally for 20 to 100 years, and Dent would add younger ones to continue the sequence. 

The site provides not just general data on forest regrowth but in-depth demographic information over time, says Robin Chazdon, a professor emeritus of ecology and evolutionary biology at the University of Connecticut who collaborated with Denslow when she established the plots. “It tells you more about the actual processes that are happening in the site,” she says. 

For example, previous research had shown that fast-growing “pioneer trees,” the first to thrive in the damaged land, are eventually overtaken by larger carbon-storing trees. Dent’s research helped fill in gaps about the mechanics of how this happens—or doesn’t happen—in individual cases. In the Gustavia-dominated patch, for instance, stubborn grasses planted by cattle ranchers smothered most other trees before they could take root. These trees can hang around, crowding out the light, for 150 years, blocking the second wave of large-trunked trees. 

To plant or not to plant

Dent found herself well placed for the massive influx of interest in reforestation that began in 2015. She’d already become a principal investigator for 2ndFor, an international research network aiming to learn how best to manage secondary forests. Using data gathered from the Barro Colorado plots, the team authored a 2016 paper in Nature showing that a hectare of naturally regenerated secondary forest can capture 11 times as much carbon each year as an old-growth one, with young trees absorbing it quickly as they compete to grow toward the sun. 

Then, in a 2022 study published by the Royal Society, Dent and colleagues showed that locations such as Barro Colorado are among the best-case scenarios for what can be achieved without planting a single seed. Clearings are often surrounded by lush environments filled with birds, bats, and other animals, all of which help tree cover regain old-growth levels of richness and abundance within a few decades. Using data from Panama and Brazil, Dent published a follow-up in 2024 showing that plots with as little as 35% of tree cover can regenerate as forest. 

“Having these long-term mapped forest plots is really valuable,” says Liza Comita, a professor of tropical forest ecology at Yale University, who is collaborating with Dent on projects that translate her findings into action. “It provides this really nice research infrastructure where you can build projects on top of that.” 

In Panama, Dent works with nonprofits and carbon-crediting schemes to fast-track recovery. They’ve mapped corridors to reconnect forest fragments and made plans to reintroduce animals in “silent forests” that have lost much of their wildlife. They’re also working to replant tree species that can accelerate growth—what Comita calls assisted natural regeneration. Leaving plots alone may seem like the simpler option, but it can’t be done everywhere, says Dent. Many sites are too degraded. 

Clearings are often surrounded by lush environments filled with birds, bats, and other animals, all of which helps tree cover regain old-growth ­levels of richness.

The two are working with the London-based carbon-crediting startup Ponterra to develop solutions for a region of southern Panama where remnant forests line the edges of abandoned ranches. Such sites almost always need some intervention, Comita explains. Many demand hands-on actions, such as enrichment planting. 

Today, the questions projects like Ponterra are asking are closer to her own research, says Dent. For instance, they want to understand if solitary standing trees, often left by ranchers to shade cows, help sites regenerate faster. Those insights can help Ponterra sell high-quality credits and avoid the embarrassing pitfalls that can lead fresh plantations to literally go up in smoke. While credits can be bought for as little as $5 per metric ton, corporate giants such as Microsoft—one of Ponterra’s clients—have paid more than 10 times as much for high-quality removal.

There are plenty of places where a level of natural regeneration can work well. So far, millions of hectares of rainforest are naturally regenerating in Brazil, according to the Brazilian Restoration and Reforestation Observatory. Still, Dent is mystified as to why the people in charge of large-scale projects continue to think the best solution is the one that imposes humans’ will on the landscape. 

The conversation may be shifting. As droughts hit Latin America, policymakers and carbon creditors might be forced to face the shortcomings of cookie-cutter plantations. “You have much reduced resilience in the system when it comes to extreme events like droughts or floods or extreme heat or pathogens,” Dent says. The coming year’s “mega El Niño” could be a moment of reckoning, she says: “I think there’s an increasing recognition that we can’t just plant trees. We have to rebuild a system.” 

Matthew Ponsford is a freelance reporter based in London.

articles.title: The Saturation Trap and the Subjectivity of Intervention Timing: Why Affect-Based Triggers and LLM Judges Fail to Time Interventions on Autonomous Agents
articles.text:
arXiv:2606.04296v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: As autonomous AI agents move from conversational systems to long-horizon software execution, runtime safety layers that decide when to interrupt an agent have become essential. We study this timing problem using a continuous 18-dimensional affective-dynamics engine (HEART) as a diagnostic probe, evaluating four intervention trigger families - absolute state thresholds, composite state-action patterns, regex reasoning-feature extraction, and zero-shot LLM-as-judge - against human-annotated intervention points on SWE-bench-Verified debugging traces. We report three findings. First, a State Saturation Trap: modeled frustration quickly crosses the threshold and stays at its maximum (v2 erratum: the observer could not register recovery; decay never ran), converting threshold-on-state triggers from moment detectors into near-constant indicators that fire on 39-83% of actions across five trajectories. Second, a capability-and-context floor for LLM judges: a small model(gpt-5.4-mini) never fires, while frontier and cross-vendor models escape the zero-firing floor only with full-trajectory context, reaching only F1 0.17-0.40 at up to 90x the cost. Third, and most importantly, the supervised target is not reproducible among humans: three trained annotators using the same rubric on a 56-action trajectory agree on where to intervene only slightly above chance (location Krippendorff's alpha = +0.047; best pairwise Cohen's kappa = +0.349) and not at all on intervention type (pause degenerate; clarify below chance; reflect only alpha = +0.226). We conclude that intervention timing is a low-reliability construct, making single-annotator F1 an unsuitable optimization target. Our contribution is the joint mapping of this problem across human inter-rater reliability, four detector architectures, a cross-model LLM-judge sweep, and a reproduced saturation effect, rather than any single detector's accuracy.

articles.title: Model-agnostic Knowledge Augmented Machine Learning for Weakly Annotated Bioimaging Data
articles.text:
arXiv:2610.13637v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Machine learning models are increasingly used for automated feature extraction from weakly annotated bioimaging data, such as microscopy and cytomorphology images. Due to the sole dependency of automated feature extraction, existing methods yield inconsistent classification performance across weakly annotated datasets. Here, we propose a model-agnostic knowledge augmentation method that enables ML models to exploit domain knowledge beyond what automated feature extraction can capture. The proposed approach improves classification performance across seven ML architectures. When integrated with masked autoencoder-based self-supervised learning, our method achieves the strongest overall performance, improving precision by 2.9% over the next-best method on three in-house microscopy datasets and by an average of 6.8% across three public cytomorphology benchmarks. We perform nucleus-level classification based on mislocalization of TAR DNA-binding protein 43 (TDP-43) from the nucleus to the cytoplasm, a phenotype linked to Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS), using three independent microscopy datasets of motor neurons derived from human induced pluripotent stem cells. Accurate quantification of this phenotype at scale remains challenging and may contribute to inconsistencies across studies. Application of the best-performing model to these microscopy datasets reveals biological interpretations related to ALS, including dose-dependent effects of the proteasomal stressor, MG132, and the oxidative stressor, sodium arsenite (SA), on TDP-43 mislocalization, variable pathology in motor neurons from sporadic and familial ALS donors, and a lack of protection of the pharmacological compounds, edaravone and niclosamide, against SA-induced TDP-43 mislocalization. Together, our pipeline enables in-vitro cellular image analysis to advance understanding of ALS-associated pathology and potential treatments.

articles.title: Bistable by Construction: Wall-Clock-Calibrated State Monitors Have No Moment-Detection Regime at Agent Cadence
articles.text:
arXiv:2606.19386v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Runtime monitors for autonomous agents commonly threshold an accumulated internal state - a behavioural baseline, a drift statistic, or, in our prior work, a modelled affective state. We previously reported a State Saturation Trap: threshold-on-state triggers over a continuous affect engine become near-constant alarms on SWE-bench debugging agents (Modgil 2026). A post-release audit found the engine received dt=0 between actions, so its exponential decay never operated: the published trap is a pure-accumulator result. We correct the record (erratum, v2) and treat the flaw as an experiment. The key variable it exposes is whether a monitor's dynamics are calibrated in sample time (per observation, as in CUSUM) or wall-clock time (half-lives in seconds, as in affect models and EMA baselines). On fixed-rate streams these coincide; on agent streams, where inter-action time varies by orders of magnitude, they do not. A pre-registered sweep over uniform intervals (dt in {0..600}s) on 20 trajectories shows the wall-clock level trigger has two regimes: at dt<=1s a constant alarm (20/20; median 18 firings); at dt>=60s silent. Every critical dt lies in (1,30]s. A scriptable gpt-5.4-mini agent loop measures latency at median 1.53s (p90 2.33s), inside the trap regime, vindicating the empirical finding under a corrected mechanism. The structure is a property of the calibration class, not the engine: a minimal wall-clock accumulator over the raw error stream reproduces the same cliff, while a sample-time CUSUM over the identical stream is exactly dt-invariant (20/20). A rising-edge trigger with hysteresis fires 0-3 times per trajectory in every condition. We conclude that wall-clock-calibrated leaky-integrator monitors admit no regime in which they act as moment detectors on agent streams; transition detection escapes the trap at every cadence, but does not recover human intervention timing.
